# 1 Executive summary

The last full EBS pollock assessment was completed in 2024 ([Ianelli et al.
2024](#ref-ianelli2024safe)). A catch report was prepared in 2025 ([Alaska Fisheries Science Center,
National Marine Fisheries Service 2025](#ref-afsc2025pollockcatch)). Changes in this assessment were
described relative to 2024.

This executive summary presents Model 26.0 (Rceattle), the base case model for this assessment and its
Tier 3 harvest recommendations. Model 23.0 (ADMB), accepted in 2024, provided the comparison with
the previous assessment.

## 1.1 Changes in assessment inputs

Catch, fishery age compositions, survey indices and age compositions, and weight-at-age schedules
were updated since 2024. [Section 2.1.1](#changes-inputs-detail) described the years, sources
and data treatments.

## 1.2 Changes in assessment methods

Model 26.0 implemented the age-structured assessment in Rceattle and used fixed weight-at-age
schedules estimated by a separate random-effects model. In contrast, Model 23.0 estimated cohort
and year effects on weight-at-age within the assessment. Uncertainty intervals for Model 26.0
exclude uncertainty in the separately estimated weight-at-age schedules. [Section
2.1.2](#changes-methods-detail) described these changes from Model 23.0.

## 1.3 Summary of results

The estimated female spawning biomass (SSB) was 3.057 million t (2.489–3.754 million t, confidence interval).

The stock was above MSST in 2026 and was not approaching an overfished condition ([Section 9](#sec-status-determination)). All risk categories were Level 1, supporting maximum ABC ([Section 8](#sec-risk-table-abc)).

## 1.4 SSC and Plan Team requests {#sec-responses}

The September 2026 Plan Team requested the following work:

- Present Model 26.0 for management use and Model 23.0 for continuity; both were compared in this assessment.
- Examine age-1 BTS selectivity and the influence of BTS variability on retrospective patterns. Additional selectivity and data-influence tests were outside the scope of this assessment.
- Extend the simulation self-test and examine retrospective patterns in time-varying selectivity. The completed simulation experiment and its limitations were described in [Section 6.3.1](#sec-model260-selftest).
- Present retrospective results for Models 23.0 and 26.0 side by side. Matched runs were completed and compared; both models showed similar spawning-biomass retrospective patterns ([Appendix A](#sec-prior-ssc)).
- Document age-composition weighting and evaluate residual patterns. Selected sample sizes, one-step-ahead residuals and Francis comparisons were presented in the assessment.
- Continue development of the Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile; we developed a draft using AI to compile and coordinate information from disparate sources ([Appendix B](#sec-esp-2026-appendix)).

Earlier SSC requests address model development, uncertainty, survey treatment and composition
weighting. The individual requests and responses were presented in [Appendix A](#sec-prior-ssc).

# 2 Introduction

## 2.1 General

Walleye pollock (*Gadus chalcogrammus*; hereafter referred to as pollock) were broadly distributed
throughout the North Pacific with the largest concentrations found in the eastern Bering Sea (EBS).
Also known as Alaska pollock, this species continues to play important roles ecologically and
economically.

### 2.1.1 Changes in assessment inputs {#changes-inputs-detail}

The 2026 assessment updates the accepted December 2024 assessment; the 2025 document was a catch
report. Updated inputs included annual catches from 1991 onward, fishery age compositions for
2024--2025, BTS indices and age compositions for 2025--2026, the 2026 ATS index and provisional age
composition, and AVO indices through 2026. Historical BTS estimates were also revised.
Spatiotemporal survey estimation continued the approach adopted in 2024; the current biomass-index
and abundance-at-age products used sdmTMB ([Anderson et al. 2025](#ref-anderson2025sdmtmb)) and
tinyVAST ([Thorson et al. 2025](#ref-thorson2025tinyvast)), respectively.

The 2024--2025 fishery age compositions used year-specific FT-NIRS-to-traditional-microscopic-age
conversions, with likelihood sample sizes of 578 and 530. The provisional 2026 ATS age composition
applied the BTS age--length key to expanded ATS length distributions that extend to 0.5 m above
the seafloor. The full 2026 ATS age dataset was expected in 2027.

Fishery weight-at-age retained the fixed 1964--1990 schedule and annual observation means for
1991--2025. A separate random-effects model fitted to fishery and BTS weights through 2025 supplied
2026 predictions and 2027--2028 forecasts; its fit omitted the 2026 BTS observations. Population
weights used BTS means through 2026, including revised historical estimates. Spawning weights at ages
3--15+ used fitted 2024--2025 A-season weights and a 2026 projection, retaining the previous ages
1--2 schedule. [Section 4](#sec-data) and [Appendix G](#sec-ftnir-appendix) and [Appendix
H](#sec-bts-spatiotemporal-appendix) described the data treatments and their uncertainty.

### 2.1.2 Changes in assessment methods {#changes-methods-detail}

The main assessment-method change was the transition from the ADMB implementation of Model 23.0 to
the Rceattle implementation of Model 26.0. Weight-at-age was estimated in a separate random-effects
model and used as fixed schedules, whereas Model 23.0 estimated cohort and year effects within the
assessment. Model 26.0 uncertainty therefore conditions on the estimated weights. Natural mortality
and catchability assumptions retained the previous treatment. The configuration comparisons,
diagnostics and sensitivities evaluate the effects of the data updates and implementation change
([Section 5](#sec-approach), [Section 6](#sec-results) and [Appendix I](#review-and-source-record)).

## 2.2 Review of Life History

In the EBS, pollock generally spawn during March--May and in relatively localized regions during
specific periods ([Bailey 2000](#ref-bailey2000)). Generally spawning begins nearshore north of
Unimak Island in March and April and later near the Pribilof Islands (Bacheler et al.
([2010](#ref-bacheler2010))). Females spawn in batches with up to 10 batches of eggs per female per
year (during the peak spawning period). Eggs and larvae of EBS pollock are planktonic for a period
of about 90 days and appear to be sensitive to environmental conditions. These conditions likely
affect their dispersal into favorable areas (for subsequent separation from predators) and also
affect general food requirements for over-wintering survival (Gann et al. ([2016](#ref-gann2015)),
Heintz et al. ([2013](#ref-heintz2013)), Hunt Jr. et al. ([2011](#ref-hunt2011)), Ciannelli et al.
([2004](#ref-ciannelli2004))). Duffy-Anderson et al. ([2016](#ref-duffy2016)) provide a review of
the early life history of EBS pollock.

Throughout their range juvenile pollock feed on a variety of planktonic crustaceans, including
calanoid copepods and euphausiids. In the EBS shelf region, one-year-old pollock are found
throughout the water column, but also commonly occur in the NMFS bottom trawl survey. Ages 2 and 3
year old pollock are rarely caught in summer bottom trawl survey gear and are more common in the
midwater zone as detected by mid-water acoustic trawl surveys. Younger pollock are generally found
in the more northern parts of the survey area and appear to move to the southeast as they aged
(Buckley et al. ([2009](#ref-buckley2009))). Euphausiids, principally *Thysanoessa inermis* and *T.
raschii*, are among the most important prey items for pollock in the Bering Sea (Livingston
([1991](#ref-livingston1991)); Lang et al. ([2000](#ref-lang2000)); Brodeur et al.
([2002](#ref-brodeur2002)); Ciannelli et al. ([2004](#ref-ciannelli2004)); Lang et al.
([2005](#ref-lang2005))). Pollock diets become more piscivorous with age, and cannibalism has been
commonly observed in this region. Buckley et al. ([2016](#ref-buckley2015)) showed that diet composition varies
with pollock size and geographic area. Fish prey became more important with increasing pollock size, especially on the northwestern
outer shelf.

## 2.3 Stock structure {#sec-stock-structure-life-history}

Stock structure for EBS pollock was evaluated in Ianelli et al. ([2015](#ref-ianelli2015)). In that
review past work on genetics (e.g., Bailey et al. ([1999](#ref-bailey1999)), Canino et al.
([2005](#ref-canino2005))) provided insight on genetic differentiation. The investigation also
compared synchrony in year-classes and growth patterns by region. Pollock samples from areas
including Zhemchug Canyon, Japan, Prince William Sound, Bogoslof, Shelikof, and the northern Bering
Sea were processed and results presented in Ianelli et al. ([2021](#ref-ianelli2021)). Genetics
research at the AFSC ([Ianelli et al. 2023](#ref-ianelli2023a)) indicated that genetic groups mostly
aligned with current stock-management delineations. The Aleutian Islands and Bogoslof stocks showed
subtle differentiation from the Gulf of Alaska stocks.

# 3 Fishery and management history

Directed foreign fishing began in 1964. US vessels entered the fishery in 1980, and it became fully
domestic by 1988. The domestic observer program formally began in 1990; later monitoring
developments included electronic monitoring on participating catcher vessels and biological sampling
during offloading ([Ianelli et al. 2024](#ref-ianelli2024safe)). The directed fishery primarily used
pelagic trawl gear, with inshore, catcher/processor and mothership sectors. The historical catch and
adopted harvest-limit series was continued through 2026 in [Table 1](#tbl-catch-management-history).

[Table 1](#tbl-catch-management-history) showed updated annual assessment catches of 1,311,261 t
in 2024 and 1,326,216 t in 2025. Excluding Bogoslof (reporting area 518) accounted for the
difference from the broader AKFIN Answers totals for these years: 22.76 t in 2024 and 63.43 t in
2025. The October 22 Alaska Region catch report listed 1,297,206 t for the Bering Sea subarea
through October 17, 2026 ([National Marine Fisheries Service Alaska Region 2026a](#ref-noaa2026cas)).
Table 1 showed the annual estimate of 1,312,505 t, rounded from the assessment input of 1,312,504.58 t.

For 2026, the adopted ABC and OFL were 2,036,000 and 2,496,000 t. The Bering Sea subarea TAC
increased from 1,375,000 to 1,389,500 t after inseason reallocations. The August allocations
included 139,400 t for Community Development Quota (CDQ) directed fishing and 46,000 t for
incidental catch. Bering Sea catch totals included CDQ directed catch and incidental catch, including
incidental CDQ catch. Bogoslof and Aleutian Islands catches were reported separately ([National
Marine Fisheries Service 2026a](#ref-noaa2026specifications), [2026c](#ref-noaa2026reallocation)).

The directed pollock allowance was allocated 45% to the A season (January 20--June 10) and 55% to the
B season (June 10--November 1). The non-CDQ allowance was divided among the inshore (50%),
catcher/processor (40%) and mothership (10%) sectors. In the Steller sea lion conservation area,
each sector may catch up to 28% of its annual directed allowance before noon April 1 ([National
Marine Fisheries Service 2026a](#ref-noaa2026specifications)). The Winter Herring Savings Area
(58--60° N, 172--175° W) was closed to directed pollock trawling, including CDQ fishing, from
September 30, 2026, to March 1, 2027 ([National Marine Fisheries Service
2026b](#ref-noaa2026herringclosure)).

Area restrictions, allocations, monitoring, and incentives were used to reduce prohibited species
catch in the EBS pollock fishery. [Table 2](#tbl-management-measures) summarized major management
changes. Industry cooperatives used rolling-hotspot closures to move fishing away from areas of high
salmon bycatch. These voluntary programs began for chum salmon in 2001 and Chinook salmon in 2002.
Amendment 84, implemented in 2007, allowed participating vessels to use approved intercooperative
bycatch-reduction agreements in place of specified fixed salmon-area closures ([National Marine
Fisheries Service 2007](#ref-noaa2007am84), [2023](#ref-noaa2023salmonhistory)).

Amendment 91 established Chinook salmon bycatch limits and incentives to reduce bycatch while
allowing the pollock TAC to be harvested. Implemented in the 2011 fishery, it combined a 60,000-fish
annual prohibited species catch (PSC) limit with incentive plan agreements and a 47,591-fish
performance standard. A sector that exceeds its share of the standard in three of seven consecutive
years receives a lower allocation in all subsequent years. Amendment 110, implemented in 2016,
strengthened Chinook and chum avoidance and tied Chinook limits to salmon returns in western Alaska.
When the State of Alaska's index for the Kuskokwim, Unalakleet and Upper Yukon systems was 250,000
fish or less, the following year's PSC limit and performance standard fall to 45,000 and 33,318
fish, respectively. The index first applied to the 2017 fishery ([National Marine Fisheries Service
2010](#ref-noaa2010am91), [2016](#ref-noaa2016am110)).

NOAA Fisheries' North Pacific Groundfish and Halibut Observer Program provided the salmon counts
used to monitor PSC limits in the Bering Sea pollock fishery. Regulations required vessels to retain
salmon until observers can count them at at-sea processors or during offloading. Catcher vessels
carry an observer or an electronic monitoring (EM) system, and shoreside observers count salmon in
deliveries ([National Marine Fisheries Service Alaska Regional Office
2025](#ref-noaa2025electronicmonitoringalaska)). The Alaska Fisheries Science Center's Genetics
Program analyzes tissue samples collected by observers to identify the salmon stocks caught as
bycatch. These stock-composition estimates helped assess impacts on salmon populations and guide
avoidance measures ([NOAA Fisheries salmon bycatch
monitoring](https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/alaska/bycatch/chinook-salmon-bycatch-management-alaska)).
Genetic sampling of the 2015 Chinook bycatch was described by ([Guthrie et al.
2017](#ref-guthrie2017chinook2015)).

## 3.1 Fishery conditions {#sec-fishery-conditions}

The A-season fishery targeted pre-spawning pollock and supported roe production. Fishing had
historically concentrated north and west of Unimak Island and along the shelf toward the Pribilof
Islands, with access affected by ice, weather and fish distribution. The summer--fall B-season
fishery followed changes in fish availability across the shelf. Salmon-avoidance measures and vessel
choices also influenced where fishing occurred. Available observer data suggested good fishing conditions
in the 2026 A season; later in the B season fishing moved farther north and pollock of desirable
sizes were less available.

The weekly reporting-area data in [Table 3](#tbl-catch-area-season) sum to 1,267,543 t through
October 17, 2026: 604,041 t in the A season and 663,501 t in the B season. This series provided
the seasonal and area split used here. Its total was 29,663 t below the Alaska Region catch report
for the same cutoff; the sources had not been reconciled.

[Table 4](#tbl-catch-retained-discarded) summarized annual retained and discarded catch. The 2026 total was 1,312,505 t, including 8,997 t discarded (0.7%).

Nominal pollock catch per tow-hour was generally higher in the A season than in the B season, with
A-season peaks in 2019 and 2023 ([Figure 1](#fig-nominal-seasonal-cpue)). Species-specific patterns
differ: A-season Chinook rates peaked in 2006--2007, whereas the chum salmon series had its largest
B-season rates in 2005 and 2017. Herring and sablefish each had a pronounced peak in 2020, in the A
and B seasons respectively. These were nominal rates for available pollock-dominated EBS hauls,
calculated from summed catch and valid tow-hours with panel-specific units.

Estimated catch numbers for both sexes decline to a trough in 2009, rise again during the 2010s and
reach their largest annual totals in 2021 ([Figure 2](#fig-catch-numbers-sex-season)). B-season
numbers generally exceed A-season numbers within each sex, and female annual catch numbers decline
from 1,075.8 million fish in 2023 to 916.7 million in 2025, while male catch numbers decline from
1,218.9 million to 952.6 million. Catch numbers were expressed in thousands of fish.

The cumulative monthly depiction showed whether A-season fishing activity shifted toward earlier
or later months within the year. Cumulative catch through April stays near 40% of annual specified
TAC over much of 2000--2017 and near 44% from 2018 onward ([Figure 3](#fig-cumulative-catch-tac)).
In 2026 the cumulative shares were 6.69%, 23.14%, 39.42% and 43.72% at the end of January, February,
March and April, respectively. Monthly totals were based on weekly catch reports and the specified
annual TAC before quota transfers. These observations cover the first four months of the year; the A
season continued through June 10.

As expected, A-season roe production exceeded B-season production throughout the 2000--2026 series
([Figure 4](#fig-roe-production)). A-season production peaks in 2006 and again in 2019, declines
through 2021 and rose from 2022 to 2026. The latest A-season value was 19,092.9 t of roe. The 2025
B-season total was 1,796 t; the 2026 total of 406 t covers June--October and represented a
partial-season estimate. The broader BSAI fishery's catch, vessel participation and market context
were summarized in the [ESP socioeconomic tables](#esp2026-economic-observations).

### 3.1.1 Recent spatial catch patterns

The seasonal maps compared 2024--2026 using the available catch-location records
([Figure 5](#fig-spatial-catch-a); [Figure 6](#fig-spatial-catch-b)). A-season maps cover January
20--June 9. B-season maps used June 10--September 18 in every year, matching the 2026 data cutoff.
Vertical bar heights showed catch tons. The rotated, elevated view separated neighboring columns. Each
season used a fixed vertical scale across its three years, with a 10,000-t reference column in each
panel. The vertical scales differ between seasons.

A-season fishing remained concentrated on the southeastern shelf, with more catch extending westward
in 2025. The share of available observed catch west of 170°W increased from 15% in 2024 to 39% in
2025, then returned to 15% in 2026. The catch-weighted mean latitude changed from 56.07°N to 56.43°N
and 56.19°N, respectively. The 2026 pattern therefore shifted back toward the southeastern grounds
relative to 2025.

The B-season distribution extended farther north and west in 2025--2026 than in 2024. The share of
catch north of 58°N increased from 54% in 2024 to 75% in 2025 and 79% in 2026. The share west of
170°W rose from 76% to about 92% in both later years. Catch-weighted mean latitude was 57.66°N in
2024, 58.56°N in 2025 and 58.52°N in 2026. Thus, the recent northward shift persisted in 2026, while
the catch-weighted mean longitude moved eastward relative to 2025, from 174.65°W to 173.26°W.

### 3.1.2 Fleet dispersion

Fleet dispersion described how widely separated fishing locations were within a day
([Figure 7](#fig-fleet-dispersion-current)). Following the 2024 assessment, we calculated the
great-circle distance between each unique pair of tows made on the same day, separately for
catcher-processors and observed catcher vessels. Distance sums and pair counts were then pooled by
year and season. Days with more tow pairs contribute more to the seasonal average. Larger values
indicate a more dispersed pattern of observed fishing locations; smaller values indicated greater
concentration.

A-season dispersion increased from 47.8 nautical miles in 2024 to 68.8 in 2025, then declined to
36.5 in 2026. This change was consistent with the 2025 westward extension and the more concentrated
southeastern pattern in 2026 shown in the catch maps. For B-season records through September 18 in
each year, dispersion declined from 78.5 nautical miles in 2024 to 67.8 in 2025 and 56.5 in 2026.
Thus, the observed B-season fishing locations became more concentrated even as much of the catch
remained farther north than in 2024. A shift in fishing location and a change in spatial spread
described different aspects of fleet behavior.

Changes in the mix of observed vessels, bycatch avoidance and fishing conditions can influence this
index, so it should be interpreted together with catch distribution and catch rates.

### 3.1.3 Seasonal changes in fish size

Mean fish weight was the pollock weight divided by the corresponding fish count. Weight-bin
distributions showed how the sizes encountered by the fishery changed over time
([Figure 8](#fig-seasonal-mean-weight)).

The dominant A-season mean-weight bin increased from 550 g in 2023 to 600 g in 2024--2025 and 700 g
in 2026. For the B season, the dominant bin increased from 450 g in 2023 to 550 g in 2024 and 700 g
in 2025, then shifted to 450 g in the available 2026 records. This recent contrast was consistent
with the reported difficulty finding larger pollock during the 2026 B season. Changes in these
distributions can reflect growth, recruitment, the areas fished and the mixture of vessels
represented in the observations.

Weekly displays showed how size patterns developed within the A-season and B-season windows
([Figure 9](#fig-seasonal-weekly-weight-a); [Figure 10](#fig-seasonal-weekly-weight-b)).

## 3.2 Bycatch {#sec-bycatch}

Pacific ocean perch (3,995 t) and Pacific cod (3,315 t) were the largest bycatch categories in the
pollock fishery in 2025, followed by flathead sole (1,813 t). Preliminary 2026 estimates through
October 24 were 2,412 t of Pacific ocean perch, 6,549 t of Pacific cod, and 3,367 t of flathead
sole. See [Table 6](#tbl-fmp-species-in-pollock).

Pollock catch in identified non-pollock fisheries declined from 46,996 t in 2024 to 29,263 t in
2025. Rock sole, yellowfin sole, and Pacific cod fisheries accounted for 10,776 t, 8,710 t, and
6,427 t, respectively, in 2025. The preliminary 2026 total through October 31 was 34,729 t; the
different cutoffs and partial-year coverage qualify comparisons with the other bycatch tables. See
[Table 7](#tbl-pollock-in-other-fisheries).

Prohibited-species bycatch in the midwater pollock fishery was summarized in
[Table 8](#tbl-prohibited-species-catch). Chinook catches increased from 8,034 fish in 2024 to
19,702 in 2025, and non-Chinook catches increased from 34,888 to 142,809 fish. Halibut mortality
rose from 22 to 50 t. Preliminary 2026 catches through October 24 were 14,503 Chinook,
145,788 non-Chinook, and 43 t of halibut mortality. The 2024 assessment also included trips
classified as bottom pollock, where pollock was the main species in the catch, outside the main
directed pollock fishery; the current table was restricted to the midwater pollock trip target.

Jellyfish dominated the selected nontarget-species catch by weight. Estimated jellyfish catch
declined from 4,402 t in 2024 to 1,769 t in 2025. Miscellaneous fish contributed 99 t in 2025, with
smaller catches in each of the other displayed groups. Preliminary jellyfish catch through October
24, 2026 was 4,418 t. These catch estimates described fishery encounters and should be interpreted
with fishing effort, distribution, and reporting coverage. See [Table
9](#tbl-nontarget-species-bycatch).

# 4. Assessment data {#sec-data}

Fishery catch data begin in 1964, whereas the BTS began in 1982 and the ATS in 1994 for the purposes
of this assessment (see the table below). Fishery age compositions were available through 2025. The 2026 BTS age estimates and provisional
ATS age compositions were described separately below.

::: {#table-003 .report-table .unnumbered data-table="tables/003-table-003.csv"}

:::

## 4.1 Fishery data {#fishery-catch-and-age-compositions}

### 4.1.1 Catch {#sec-fishery-catch}

Annual catch rose from about 0.175 million t in 1964 to the series maximum of 1.875 million t in
1972 ([Figure 11](#fig-catch-history)). Catch subsequently fluctuated, fell to 0.811 and 0.810
million t in 2009 and 2010, respectively, and recovered to 1.326 million t in 2025. The 2026 records
total 1.268 million t through October 17 and represented a partial year. Records before 1991 provided
annual totals; later records distinguished the A-season and northwest and southeast B-season catches.

The annual assessment catch included retained and discarded commercial pollock across gears and
targets in the Bering Sea, including CDQ catches but excluding the separately reported Bogoslof and
Aleutian Islands catches. The catch update used the catch estimates for 1991--2026, with pre-1991
model inputs retained. The revised totals were 1,311,260.74 t in 2024, 1,326,215.61 t in 2025 and
1,312,504.58 t in 2026. Noncommercial removals remain separately
documented in [Appendix C](#sec-other-removals).

### 4.1.2 Age compositions {#sec-fishery-age-compositions}

Fishery catch-at-age estimates for 1964--2025 were summarized in
[Table 5](#tbl-fishery-catch-at-age). Ages 15 and older were pooled as 15+. Where complete annual
catch numbers were unavailable, we calculated numbers at age from the assessment proportions, annual
fishery weight-at-age and catch biomass.

The fishery catch-at-age history for 1991--2025 ([Figure 12](#fig-fishery-catch-at-age-history))
showed strong year classes progressing through successive ages. The 2018 year class was highlighted
from age 2 in 2020 through age 7 in 2025. It accounted for the largest catch numbers at age in
2023--2025, shifting from age 5 to age 7 over those years. The display pooled ages 10 and older;
the assessment retained ages 1--14 and 15+.

We estimated fishery age compositions from biological samples collected by at-sea observers and
during shore-side offloading. The sampling records included fish measured for length frequencies,
paired weight--length measurements, and age estimates ([Table 10](#tbl-fishery-length-samples);
[Table 11](#tbl-fishery-weight-length-samples); [Table 12](#tbl-fishery-age-samples)). The
processing kept recent unsexed fish separate rather than assigning them to males or females. Within
each sex and sampling stratum, we expand length frequencies to the associated catch biomass using
mean weight at length. Age--length keys allocated the expanded numbers to ages; we then sum the
numbers across strata and sexes and normalize them to give annual proportions ([Kimura
1989](#ref-kimura1989); [Barbeaux et al. 2005](#ref-barbeaux2005); [Ianelli et al.
2024](#ref-ianelli2024safe)). Earlier assessments provided the pre-1991 age compositions. For the
2026 assessment update, the 2024--2025 fishery samples were processed in strata defined as January--May across Bering Sea areas, followed by
June--December split into northwest (NMFS reporting areas 520 and above) and southeast (areas below
520).

A hierarchical bootstrap resampled sampling units within fishery strata and length and age
observations within those units, preserving their sampling links. Its composition precision estimates informed the selected likelihood sample sizes:
443, 578 and 530 for 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively. They represented effective information for
fitting the annual proportions, rather than numbers of fish measured or aged
([Section 4.3.1](#sec-weights)). The model fitted annual sex-combined proportions at ages 1--14 and
15+. Fishery age observations ended in 2025.

The 2024--2025 age-estimate data were from pelagic trawl fisheries. For 2025, ages predicted by
Fourier-transform near-infrared spectroscopy (FT-NIRS) of otoliths were converted to an independent
traditional microscopic-ageing (TMA) basis using 668 paired estimates. The FT-NIRS prediction model
was identified as a00-d3 ([Appendix G](#sec-ftnir-appendix)). Within each FT-NIRS age, the paired
observations define the proportions assigned to each tester age. These probabilities redistribute
the catch-expanded numbers among ages while preserving their total. No paired tester observations were available for fish assigned FT-NIRS age 13, so the conversion
probabilities for this age were the averages of those for FT-NIRS ages 12 and 14. The
likelihood used the selected input sample size of 530. Uncertainty in the conversion key and the
age-13 interpolation was additional to the sampling uncertainty represented by that input weight.

The 2024 fishery age composition was converted to the independent TMA basis using 693 paired
reader--tester observations. The conversion for age 13 used age offsets from paired observations
at ages 9--12; [Appendix G](#sec-ftnir-appendix) described this year-specific treatment.

### 4.1.3 Weight-at-age {#sec-fishery-weights}

Mean weight-at-age connected the assessment's estimates of fish numbers to catch biomass and harvest
projections. Seasonal and spatial differences in fish condition and fishery distribution affect
these means. Fishery sampling was therefore organized by season and area, with stratum estimates
combined using the corresponding catch information. Completed-year observations provided the basis
for estimating weights for the observation year and forecasting the weights needed for future
catches.

For recent fishery samples, Fourier-transform near-infrared spectroscopy (FT-NIR) of otoliths
provided predicted ages. Year-specific paired FT-NIR and traditional morphological ageing (TMA)
observations align these predictions with the TMA age basis. Estimated abundance and biomass in each
FT-NIR age bin were redistributed using the same conditional tester-age key. Mean weight at a target
age was then converted biomass divided by converted abundance. For the 15+ group, biomass and
abundance were pooled before taking their ratio. The conversion retained each source bin's mean weight
when allocating it among tester ages. Its reported uncertainty conditions on the selected key; the
ages with paired observations and the approved tail-allocation rules were documented in [Appendix
G](#sec-ftnir-appendix).

The weight-model approach described in Section 14.5 of the 2024 assessment ([Ianelli et al.
2024](#ref-ianelli2024safe)) linked growth within cohorts to annual changes in condition. A smooth
mean age pattern defined the typical weight increments. A cohort's weight in the previous year
provided the starting point for the next age, while annual random effects allow variation in
starting weight and growth. Observed mean weights and their variances informed this model, separating
sampling precision from variability among years. The fitted model supplied predictions for missing
observations and forecasts for future years. Model 26.0 used the resulting weight schedules as fixed
biological inputs.

The annual fishery weights in [Table 28](#tbl-fishery-weights-projections) retained the historical
observational inputs through 2025, with fitted values for missing 2025 ages 13 and 14. The 2026
predictions and 2027--2028 forecasts used the standalone WtAgeRE fit. Ages 1--2 retained the 2024
inputs, and the terminal age was 15+. The fixed 1964--1990 schedule matched the historical
fishery weight-at-age series in [Ianelli et al. (2001), Table 1.9](#ref-ianelli2001).

Cohort growth and annual changes in condition linked observed weights to the schedules used for catch
and spawning projections. Observed fishery and BTS weights and the selected fishery-scale estimates
for 2014--2028 were shown in [Figure 24](#fig-waa-omit-bts2026). The forecast followed the 2026 age-3
cohort from 0.368 kg to 0.482 kg at age 4 in 2027 and 0.601 kg at age 5 in 2028. The 2026 biological
weight schedules were compared with the selected 2027 catch and spawning projection weights in
[Figure 36](#fig-model262-current-biological-schedules).

## 4.2 Survey data

### 4.2.1 Bottom-trawl survey

The AFSC bottom-trawl survey provided indices of pollock abundance and population age structure,
complementing the acoustic-trawl survey's sampling of the midwater component. Historical and recent
sampling effort was summarized in [Table 13](#tbl-bts-sampling-effort). Annual surveys began in 1979,
with standardized gear and methods from 1982 ([Ianelli et al. 2024](#ref-ianelli2024safe)). The 2025
and 2026 observations extend the 42 survey years available for the 2024 assessment to 44 observed
years during 1982--2026. The survey was absent in 2020; that year remained a gap in the observation
series. The biomass estimates and assessment CVs were listed in [Table 14](#tbl-bts-biomass).
Availability to bottom-trawl gear varied with age and vertical distribution. Ages 2--3 were often
relatively scarce in the catches because juveniles tend to occupy the water column ([Monnahan et al.
2021](#ref-monnahan2021); [O'Leary et al. 2022](#ref-oleary2022)).

Bottom temperature appears to influence the distribution of pollock available to the bottom-trawl
survey. The AKsf survey-mapping example ([Ianelli 2026](#ref-ianelli2026aksf)) places annual CPUE
distributions alongside the 0, 2 and 4 °C bottom-temperature contours for 2018, 2019 and 2021--2026
([Figure 13](#fig-bts-cpue-temperature-aksf)). High CPUE was concentrated along parts of the western
and southern shelf, with several dense patches near the 2 °C contour in 2022, 2024 and 2026. The
more extensive warm-water conditions in 2018--2019 contrast with the broader areas of cold bottom
water in later panels, while the locations and extent of the pollock concentrations also change.

These patterns suggested that temperature helped structure near-bottom habitat and survey availability,
with concentrations often near the margins of colder shelf water. Depth, prey, age composition and
vertical movements can also contribute to the pattern. The maps showed spatial associations between
survey distributions and temperature. Other environmental and biological factors may also
contribute. They used locally interpolated, density-dependent-corrected CPUE within survey coverage.
These maps illustrate survey distributions; they were not the biomass index fitted in the assessment.
The example does not identify the version of its density-dependent correction.

The standard EBS survey expanded northwest in 1987. Sampling in the separate NBS region varied
among years, while pollock distribution shifted between regions. Model-based estimates integrated
station observations, including zero catches, across the EBS and NBS and account for spatial and
temporal variation ([O'Leary et al. 2020](#ref-OLeary2020)). The biomass index used sdmTMB and
abundance at age used tinyVAST, replacing the earlier VAST implementation. The complete selected
abundance-at-age series incorporated historical revisions as well as the recent observations
([Table 15](#tbl-bts-abundance-at-age)). The regional coverage, model specifications, annual
covariance and remaining production-source qualifications were described in [Appendix
H](#sec-bts-spatiotemporal-appendix). Estimates for unsampled years were model predictions.

The BTS length distributions showed pronounced changes in the sizes represented in the survey
([Figure 14](#fig-bts-length-composition-history)). Peaks among small fish and their progression
toward larger lengths illustrate cohort growth, while the relative contribution of small and large
fish varied among years. These distributions complemented the age compositions by showing changes in
size directly.

The BTS age compositions showed changes in the ages represented in the survey and the progression of
cohorts through time ([Figure 15](#fig-bts-age-composition-history)). Highlighted bars follow the
1992, 2012 and 2018 year classes through successive ages. The blank 2020 row marks the gap when the survey was absent.

The age compositions combined traditional age readings and FT-NIRS estimates. We converted the 2026
FT-NIRS estimates to traditional ages using 307 screened paired readings ([Appendix
G](#sec-ftnir-appendix)). The conversion preserved total survey abundance and pooled ages 15 and
older into the 15+ group.

Spatiotemporal estimation of BTS weight-at-age, adopted in 2022, replaces the earlier conversion of
mean length to weight ([Indivero et al. 2023](#ref-indivero2023)). The full BTS-derived weight
schedules used for population biomass were presented in [Table 16](#tbl-bts-historical-weights); [Section 4.3](#sec-other-data) summarized the fishery and spawning weight schedules and fixed
biological assumptions. We applied the screened 2026 age key consistently to BTS weight-at-age means
and their delta-method standard errors, retaining the joint covariance treatment. We used the same
key for the provisional ATS abundance and biomass-derived weights, including the weights used to
predict the 2026 AVO index. We refitted the standalone random-effects weight-at-age model with the
revised BTS means and standard errors under the existing equations, likelihood and source-covariance
treatment, preserving fishery observations and the 2025 conversion key. These uncertainty
calculations exclude empirical age-key uncertainty. The conversion, weight calculations and
assessment use were described in [Appendix G](#sec-ftnir-treatment).

The missing 2020 survey and subsequent 2021 observation affect interpretation of the time series.
Retrospective comparisons described changes in population estimates as observations accumulated
([Section 6.1.5](#sec-paired-current-retrospectives)).

### 4.2.2 Acoustic-trawl survey {#sec-ats}

The provisional 2026 core-shelf ATS age estimates applied the BTS age--length key (ALK) to
expanded ATS length distributions that extend to 0.5 m above the seafloor. The full 2026 ATS
age dataset was expected in 2027.

Acoustic-trawl surveys (ATS) were typically conducted every other year and estimate the off-bottom
component of the pollock stock, complementing the annual BTS index of near-bottom pollock.
Historical and acoustic-trawl sampling effort was summarized in [Table 17](#tbl-ats-sampling-effort).

Estimated pollock biomass for the EBS shelf averaged about 3.202 million t since 1994, when the
revised time series began ([Table 18](#tbl-ats-biomass)). The revised estimates included the water
column down to 0.5 m above the seafloor; the historical midwater index extended to 3 m above the
seafloor. Low recruitment during the relatively warm early 2000s was subsequently reflected in lower
survey biomass during the cold period of 2006--2012 ([Honkalehto and McCarthy
2015](#ref-honkalehto2015)). With growth of the strong 2012 year class, biomass exceeded 4 million t
in 2014 and 2016, another warm period. The 2026 regional estimates included the Steller sea lion
conservation area (SCA) and the Northern Extension ([Table 19](#tbl-ats-regions)). The SCA was a
traditionally reported subset of the survey used to evaluate pollock abundance in areas considered
sensitive to Steller sea lions.

#### Historical abundance at age {#sec-ats-age-history}

The historical series showed strong pulses of age-1 fish in 1997, 2007, 2009, 2014 and 2024
([Table 20](#tbl-ats-age-history)). The provisional 2026 estimates were largest at ages 2 and 3:
3.73 and 3.96 billion fish, respectively, compared with 2.03 billion age-1 fish.

The ATS age compositions showed pulses of young fish and the progression of cohorts through successive
surveys ([Figure 16](#fig-ats-age-composition-history)). The highlighted 2018 year class appears at
age 4 in 2022, age 6 in 2024 and age 8 in 2026. Ages 2 and 3 dominated the provisional 2026
composition. Blank years represented gaps in the age-composition series.

#### 2026 survey design and results

The 2026 ATS covered the EBS shelf from approximately 60 m depth to the shelf break between 30 May
and 4 August. Core-area transects were spaced at 20 nmi; selected transects extended into the
Northern Extension at 40 nmi spacing. Survey timing was similar to 2022, with a longer duration in
2026 because of special projects. The area east of 170° W was surveyed from 30 May to 25 June, and
the area west of 170° W from 26 June to 4 August.

The 2026 core-area estimate was 12.7 billion fish and 3.682 million t of biomass
([Table 21](#tbl-ats-core-estimates)). Biomass increased by 28% relative to the 2024 estimate of
2.875 million t (11.4 billion fish). The 2026 biomass estimate was 4% below the 2022 estimate of
3.834 million t (9.67 billion fish) and 16% above the 1994--2024 survey mean of 3.176 million t.

We estimated provisional 2026 ATS age compositions by applying the FT-NIRS-based BTS
age--length key to ATS abundance in the length bins covered by the key ([Appendix G](#sec-ftnir-appendix)).
Midwater pollock were concentrated between the 100 m contour and the shelf break, particularly
northwest of Unimak Pass and between Zhemchug and Pervenets canyons. Length distributions suggested
that presumed age-1 fish (\<20 cm fork length) formed dense schools on the northwestern shelf, with
smaller concentrations east of the Pribilof Islands and near Unimak Pass. Presumed age-3+ fish
accounted for most biomass, with 74% of their biomass west of 170° W.

#### Provisional abundance at age from the 2026 BTS keys {#sec-ats-derived-ages}

We estimated provisional ages by matching ATS lengths to the 2026 BTS FT-NIRS age--length key, then
converting those ages to traditional ages using paired readings. Ages 2 and 3 dominated the
resulting distribution ([Table 22](#tbl-ats-derived-abundance); [Figure 17](#fig-ats-derived-ages)).
Fish beyond the key's length range represented less than 0.001% of core-area abundance. The
technical appendix described the keys, calibration and allocation assumptions.

#### Biomass and mean weight-at-age {#sec-ats-derived-weights}

We applied the same age keys to biomass and divided biomass by abundance to estimate mean weights at
age. The resulting mean weights were presented in [Table 23](#tbl-ats-tma-weights) and [Figure
18](#fig-ats-derived-weights).

#### Survey uncertainty and assessment treatment

We estimated ATS biomass sampling error with the established one-dimensional geostatistical method,
which accounted for spatial patterns along survey transects ([Petitgas 1993](#ref-petitgas1993);
[Walline 2007](#ref-walline2007); [Williamson and Traynor 1996](#ref-williamson1996)). The 2026
sampling error was 3.4% of estimated biomass, compared with a historical average of 4.4%. Complete
core-area coverage at 20 nmi transect spacing likely contributed to the lower error.

For assessment use, we increased the survey errors to allow for additional uncertainty, including
target strength and trawl selectivity. We scaled the assessment coefficients of variation to average
20% over 1994--2026 and assigned a value of 45% to 2000 ([Table 18](#tbl-ats-biomass)).

#### Spatial and historical patterns

The ATS index used in the assessment covered the water column down to 0.5 m above the seafloor,
while the historical heatmap showed biomass from near the surface to 3 m above the bottom
([Figure 19](#fig-ats-historical-heatmap)). Biomass was low during 2008--2012, especially in
2008--2009, and increased in 2014--2016. The maps also showed shifts in the strength and location of
concentrations along the western and southern shelf. The Northern Extension contained an additional
0.078 million t beyond the 3.682 million t core-area estimate ([Table 19](#tbl-ats-regions)).

#### Biomass time series and observation errors

The series contained 20 survey estimates between 1994 and 2026. We plotted approximate 95% sampling
intervals around each biomass estimate using the survey standard errors
([Figure 20](#fig-ats-biomass); [Table 18](#tbl-ats-biomass)). Gaps in the annual series marked
years without a survey estimate. These intervals described survey sampling variability; the
assessment used larger errors to allow for additional uncertainty.

Biomass varied strongly along the survey tracks. Concentrations were highest on parts of the western
and southern shelf and generally lower in the far north ([Figure 21](#fig-ats-transects)). The map
included the Northern Extension and showed GMT contours of mean biomass per sampling interval (tons
per EDSU). The map used approximately 10-nautical-mile cell means, with the smoothed surface
displayed within 30 km of sampled cell centers.

### 4.2.3 Acoustic vessel-of-opportunity index {#sec-avo}

The acoustic vessel-of-opportunity (AVO) index provided a relative-abundance observation for age-1
and older midwater pollock within the U.S. EEZ ([Honkalehto et al. 2011](#ref-honkalehto2011);
[Lauffenburger et al. 2025](#ref-lauffenburger2025avo)). The 2026 observations were collected at 38
kHz from 29 May to 5 August aboard the summer bottom-trawl charter vessels. The index covers the
water column from 3 m above the seabed to 16 m below the surface.

#### Annual index {#assessment-index}

Relative AVO backscatter was lowest at 0.299 in 2009 and highest at 1.55 in 2015
([Table 25](#tbl-avo-index); [Figure 22](#fig-avo-index)). It was 0.863 in 2024, 1.07 in 2025 and
1.12 in 2026, with sampling CVs of 2.72%, 5.26% and 4.55%, respectively. The 2025 and 2026 sampling
confidence intervals overlap. The display series covers 2009--2026, excluding 2020, when no
bottom-trawl survey took place. The relative AVO index divides each annual area-integrated estimate by the mean of the
17 estimates, producing a series with a mean of one. The table also showed total pollock backscatter,
in millions of square meters, with sampling errors and scaled confidence intervals. This was an acoustic
backscattering cross section, rather than geographic area ([Lauffenburger et al.
2025](#ref-lauffenburger2025avo)).

For the nine paired survey years in the 2009--2026 display period, AVO total pollock backscatter and
revised ATS biomass had a squared Pearson correlation of 0.89. This association was descriptive: AVO
covers 3 m above the seabed to 16 m below the surface, while the revised ATS index extended from 0.5
m above the seabed to 16 m below the surface. The vertical domains differed. The 2026 AVO report gave
0.90 using an ATS 2026 estimate of 3.62 million t; the comparison here used the revised ATS estimate
of 3.682 million t ([AFSC-RACE MACE 2026](#ref-afscmace2026avo)).

#### Spatial distribution and sampling coverage

Strong backscatter occurred along western EBS tracks in the recent maps, with weaker returns
interspersed along central and southeastern tracks ([Figure 23](#fig-avo-all-years)). The annual
panels used a common map extent and color scale while showing differences in track coverage.

The longer series also contained alternating strong and weak returns along the sampled shelf
([Figure 23](#fig-avo-all-years)). The year 2020 was omitted because AVO observations were
unavailable. Survey coverage and processing vary among years. Inferences about population
redistribution require comparable sampling and integration across years.

The number of observed survey intervals ranges from 5,557 in 2009 to 12,229 in 2024
([Table 26](#tbl-avo-coverage)). The percentage of sampling intervals with zero pollock backscatter fell from 56.3% in 2009
to 7.8% in 2015 and varied thereafter. It was 14.9%, 5.0% and 14.2% in 2024--2026, respectively.

The maps summarize observed pollock backscatter in approximately 20-nautical-mile cells, including
zeros. GMT gridding and contours showed the mean backscatter in m² nmi⁻² on a common color scale.
Surfaces extend up to 45 km from sampled cell centers; more distant areas remain masked. The annual
AVO index integrated backscatter over the survey area and was reported in million m². Survey coverage
and processing vary among years, so comparisons of spatial patterns depend on comparable sampling.

#### Assessment use and observation uncertainty {#sec-avo-assessment-cvs}

The AVO assessment index was 2.01 million m² in 2024, 2.50 million m² in 2025 and 2.60 million m² in
2026 ([Table 27](#tbl-avo-assessment-series)). Its 20 observations cover 2006--2026, excluding 2020.
The assessment used the newly processed 2011 and 2013 estimates and their sampling errors
([AFSC-RACE MACE 2026](#ref-afscmace2026avo)). The 2006--2008 estimates retained the legacy rescaling
described in the 2024 assessment ([Ianelli et al. 2024](#ref-ianelli2024safe)).

Survey sampling errors described one-dimensional geostatistical variability. The assessment applied
additional observation-error inflation to an arithmetic mean CV of 23% across its 20 observations.
The two newly processed years used the existing modern-year error inflation rule, followed by common
recalibration of all 20 CVs to that mean. Assessment errors differ from sampling errors and from the
ATS mean assessment CV of 20%.

For the Normal index likelihood, arithmetic observation SEs equal the assessment index
multiplied by its selected CV. For the display series, let $I_t$ denote the original index, $\bar I$
its 17-year mean and $R_t=I_t/\bar I$. The same constant rescales its index, SEs and confidence
limits, leaving the CV unchanged:

$$
\mathrm{SE}(R_t)=R_t\,\mathrm{CV}_t,\qquad
[L_t,U_t]=\frac{I_t\pm1.96\,I_t\mathrm{CV}_t}{\bar I}.
$$

The approximate 95% interval had half-width $1.96 I_t\mathrm{CV}_t$. The displayed intervals described survey sampling uncertainty with normalization
treated as a change of units; assessment error inflation was a separate model input.

## 4.3 Other data {#sec-other-data}

Model 26.0 fitted 12 annual observations of catch per unit effort (CPUE) from the Japanese trawl
fishery, 1965--1976, using fishery selectivity and weight-at-age. The 2024 assessment described
the vessel-size restriction in this series ([Ianelli et al. 2024](#ref-ianelli2024safe)).

*Fixed biological assumptions*

We retained the 2024 biological assumptions ([Ianelli et al. 2024](#ref-ianelli2024safe)). Natural
mortality was 0.9 yr⁻¹ at age 1, 0.45 yr⁻¹ at age 2 and 0.3 yr⁻¹ at ages 3--15+. Maturity at ages
1--15+ was 0, .008, .289, .641, .842, .901, .947, .963, .970, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1. The model calculated
April spawning biomass one quarter-year after the start of the year and applied a female fraction of
0.5 once to sex-combined abundance. We used a 15-by-15 identity matrix for ageing error, matching
the archived ADMB configuration. This likelihood assumption treated ages as exact after data
preparation, which used FT-NIRS age conversion and age--length keys.

All weight schedules covered ages 1--15+ for the combined sexes in kg per fish. The model used
fishery weights to calculate catch biomass, BTS weights to calculate population biomass and A-season
weights to calculate spawning biomass.

*Population and spawning weights*

Population weights used BTS observations through 2026. For spawning biomass, we replaced the older
weights at ages 3--15+ with A-season fitted values for 2024--2025 and projections for 2026. Within
the common-year comparison, this update changed the 13 values at ages 3--15+ in 2024. We retained
baseline weights at ages 1--2; age-2 maturity was .008.

*ATS and AVO weights*

We retained each historical schedule through 2024 and carried its weights forward to 2025. After
BTS-ALK and conditional TMA preparation, we calculated provisional 2026 ATS weights by dividing
biomass by the corresponding abundance. For age 15+, we pooled biomass and abundance before
division. [Appendix G](#sec-ftnir-appendix) documents which lengths the BTS key covers and which remain unallocated.
We used the 2026 ATS vector as a proxy for AVO weights, although the historical schedules differed.

[Section 4.1.3](#sec-fishery-weights) described the rationale for changing weight estimation. Weight-schedule uncertainty remained separate from the assessment's conditional parameter uncertainty.

### 4.3.1 Age-composition input sample sizes {#sec-weights}

The full-data Model 23.0 fit used fishery composition N=443, 578 and 530 for 2023, 2024 and 2025,
respectively ([Table 24](#tbl-model23-age-sample-sizes)). These likelihood sample sizes were rounded harmonic estimates of composition precision from
10,000 bootstrap replicates per year, scaled for continuity with the historical series. The
bootstrap resampled sampling units within fishery strata and observations within those units,
preserving their sampling links. ATS 2026 used N=94, and BTS retained the selected 2026 N,
shown as 131. Fishery N was fixed at 10 in each year from 1964--1977. The three
composition-likelihood multipliers were 1.

Model 26.0 fitted age compositions with a multinomial model.

One-step-ahead (OSA) residuals compared an observation with its conditional prediction after
preceding age categories were considered. The OSA and Francis comparisons document the selected
weights and observed-data residual patterns in [Section 6.1.6](#sec-francis-comparison).

# 5 Analytic approach {#sec-approach}

## 5.1 Main and comparison models

Model 26.0 was the base case model used for Tier 3 calculations and harvest recommendations. Models 23.0
and 23.2 provide comparisons with the previous assessment and the transition in model structure.
Model 26.1.2 is a sensitivity analysis that separates the early (1964--1990) and modern (1991--2026)
fisheries and estimates modern selectivity variation after integrating over annual fishery selectivity
effects. Its conditional fits and retrospective comparisons hold both process standard deviations fixed;
the modern period's value comes from the marginal model. Model 26.0 uncertainty and retrospective diagnostics are described
below. Model equations are given in [the model-equations appendix](#sec-model-equations). The
projection methodology is described in [Section 7](#sec-projections).

The cumulative data comparison holds the Model 23.0 formulation fixed; the configuration
comparison used matched updated observations to separate changes in model structure from changes
in data.

| Model | Data and purpose | Main configuration difference |
|---|---|---|
| 23.0 (ADMB) | Accepted in 2024; refitted through 2026 to measure the effects of each data update | One fishery; cohort and year effects on weight-at-age are estimated within the assessment. |
| 23.2 (ADMB bridge) | Same updated observations as the full-data 23.0 fit | Brings key features of the Rceattle formulation into ADMB, including mean recruitment and fixed weight-at-age schedules. |
| 26.0 (Rceattle) | Updated observations; basis for the 2026 assessment | Uses one fishery and fixed weight-at-age schedules. Differs from the bridge in the annual fishery-selectivity setup and its penalties. |
| 26.1.0 and 26.1.1 (Rceattle) | Same updated observations; split-fishery sensitivities | Estimate separate selectivity for the early and modern fisheries, with different penalties on declining selectivity. |
| 26.1.2 (Rceattle) | Same updated observations; split-fishery sensitivity | Estimates variation in modern selectivity after integrating over annual fishery selectivity effects. |

### 5.1.1 Model 23.0 and impact of new data {#sec-model23-data-impacts}

We added the new data to Model 23.0 in steps. First, we updated annual catches for 1991--2026
(the 2026 estimate was 1,312,504.58 t). We then updated weight-at-age and A-season spawning weights,
followed by fishery catch-at-age data and their likelihood weights.

We added survey data in the following order: bottom-trawl survey (BTS), acoustic-trawl survey
(ATS), and acoustic vessel-of-opportunity (AVO) index. The survey updates included historical
revisions and changes to observation errors. The ATS step used the provisional 2026 ages and
included all 20 entries in the separate age-1 index likelihood, including the newest year and the
inherited 2020 substitute of 350 million fish. The latter was distinct from the observed 2020
uncrewed-surface-vessel biomass estimate. The ATS age-composition likelihood used ages 2--15+
([Section 4.2.2](#sec-ats); [Section 4.2.3](#sec-avo)).

Each step included all preceding updates, so its estimated effect depended on the order in which the
data were added. The resulting 2026 estimates were summarized in
[Table 29](#tbl-model23-data-impacts), and the cumulative annual point estimates were shown in
[Figure 25](#fig-model23-data-impacts). See [Appendix F](#sec-model-equations) for the model
equations.

[Figure 26](#fig-model23-2027-increments) compared projections of 2027 spawning biomass and
abundance at ages 1--3 as each dataset was added. These diagnostics used the earlier assumed
2026 catch of 1,310,000 t. The 2026 estimates in [Table 29](#tbl-model23-data-impacts) use
1,312,504.58 t. The display starts with Catch + 2026 endpoint, followed by + Fishery age data and the
subsequent survey updates. The intervening weight-at-age and A-season spawning-weight updates remain
incorporated in the fishery-age and later fits. Abundance at ages 1--3 was measured at the start of
2027, before removals; spawning biomass included mortality to spawning time. Projection settings were
detailed in the technical supplement. See [Section 7](#sec-projections) for the management projections.

The input sequence and configuration comparison answer different questions. The former retained the
Model 23.0 formulation while adding observations and updating schedules. The latter compared
formulations on matched observations and biology ([Table 30](#tbl-updated-configuration-effects)).

Approximate distributions compared the change in spawning biomass from 2026 to 2027
([Figure 27](#fig-model23-ssb-change-density)) and the historical change in total abundance at ages
1--4 from 2025 to 2026 ([Figure 28](#fig-model23-young-n-change-density)). They showed the same
selected cumulative sequence, followed by Models 23.2 and 26.0. Their input and projection settings
were documented in the technical supplement. Each distribution retained its matching fitted-parameter
covariance between years and, for abundance, among ages. The normal approximations were conditional
on the model and biological and projection assumptions.

Adding ATS data produced the largest increase in projected 2027 female spawning biomass: from
2.685 to 2.975 million t, about 290,000 t (10.8%) above the preceding BTS step. Adding AVO data
increased it by a further 61,000 t (2.0%), to 3.036 million t. For estimated 2026 spawning biomass,
adding fishery ages produced the largest increase, about 213,000 t (8.4%). Adding ATS data reduced
the estimate by about 73,000 t (2.6%), and adding AVO data increased it by about 47,000 t (1.7%).

### 5.1.2 Model 23.2 fitted to the 2026 assessment data {#sec-model232-updated}

Model 23.2 implemented key features of the Rceattle formulation in ADMB. Compared with Model 23.0,
it used mean recruitment, estimated annual fishing mortality without the penalty on annual
deviations, and treated weight-at-age as fixed. It predicted ATS and AVO biomass from ages 2--15+;
age 1 entered the separate ATS index. With the observations held constant,
[Figure 29](#fig-model230-vs232) compared annual trajectories and approximate 95% confidence
intervals calculated from each fit's parameter covariance.

### 5.1.3 Model 26.0 fitted to the 2026 assessment data {#sec-model262-updated}

Model 26.0 fitted one fishery in Rceattle with fixed weight-at-age schedules. The comparison with
Model 23.2 used the same updated observations and biological schedules, but the implementations
differed. Model 26.0 estimated a separate 1965 fishery selectivity curve; Model 23.2 used the 1964
curve in both years. The models also differ in the penalties on changes in fishery selectivity
and in how future recruitment deviations enter estimation. [Figure 30](#fig-model232-vs262)
compared annual estimates and approximate 95% confidence intervals. The base-model fit retained its
native working likelihood, parameter bounds, selectivity forms, priors and fixed biological
assumptions; outputs were checked against the written inputs and saved native quantities.
Population-weight biomass, female spawning biomass, age-1 recruitment and maximum fishing mortality
retain distinct definitions.

### 5.1.4 Model 26.1: Early and modern domestic fisheries {#sec-model261-configuration}

The split-fishery sensitivities estimate separate selectivity curves and annual changes for the
early (1964--1990) and modern domestic (1991--2026) periods. The split changed which selectivity
curve applied to each year's catch and age composition; it does not divide the stock or reassign
catches by vessel nationality. Model 26.1.0 applied the original penalty on declining selectivity
at older ages. Model 26.1.1 reduced the penalty, and a separate comparison removed it.

Model 26.1.2 kept the reduced penalty and integrated over the annual fishery selectivity effects
when estimating the modern period's process standard deviation (SD). The early period's SD was fixed
at 0.1235; the modern period's marginal estimate was 0.582. The conditional fits used for observation
diagnostics, projections and retrospective comparisons hold both SDs at those values. Marginal-fit
confidence intervals use the curvature of the likelihood after integrating over the selectivity
effects. Local uncertainty uses the verified marginal information for Model 26.1.2; its observation
diagnostics condition on the fitted annual effects. [Section 6.2](#sec-model261-results) described
the resulting comparisons.

# 6 Results {#sec-results}

[Table 30](#tbl-updated-configuration-effects) compares estimated 2026 total biomass, female spawning
biomass, age-1 recruitment and maximum fishing mortality across the 2026 model configurations.

## 6.1 Model 26.0 assessment

Model 26.0 estimates provided the basis for the Tier 3 catch limits. We described their uncertainty
and how they changed when we removed recent years of data.
Comparisons with past assessments used each assessment's data and catch assumptions. Results from
alternative configurations, including Model 26.1.2, were presented in [Section 6.2](#sec-model261-results).

### 6.1.1 Population estimates and uncertainty {#sec-model262-current-estimates}

The Model 26.0 base case model estimated 2026 total biomass at 12.162 million t, female spawning
biomass at 3.057 million t, age-1 recruitment at 36.3 billion fish, and maximum fishing
mortality across ages at 0.299 per year ([Table 31](#tbl-model262-current-terminal-estimates)).

The approximate 95% confidence intervals used the parameter covariance from the Model 26.0 fit,
with biological schedules held fixed. [Figure 31](#fig-model262-current-full-uncertainty) showed
the annual estimates and intervals, and [Table 32](#tbl-model262-current-annual-estimates)
reported the values.

The 2026 posterior medians for total biomass, female spawning biomass and age-1 recruitment
were below their corresponding fitted point estimates. The regularized posterior used all 5,000
MCMC draws ([Table 33](#tbl-model260-regularized-posterior)). The female spawning-biomass median
was 2.946 million t (central 95% credible interval 2.450--3.584 million t), the total-biomass
median was 11.462 million t (9.215--14.719 million t), and median age-1 recruitment was
31.1518 billion fish (12.2880--91.0616 billion fish). The management calculations used
the fitted point estimates; the MCMC summaries provided a separate view of uncertainty.

[Figure 32](#fig-model262-current-numbers-uncertainty) tracked cohorts as they aged by showing
abundance at each age relative to its long-term mean, alongside the coefficient of variation.
[Table 34](#tbl-model262-current-numbers-at-age) reported the annual abundance estimates, and
[Table 35](#tbl-model262-current-terminal-numbers) reported estimates and uncertainty by age in 2026.

#### Comparison with the 2024 assessment

The 2018 year class remained the largest recruitment point estimate in both assessments
([Figure 33](#fig-recruitment-2024-current)). Model 26.0 estimated its age-1 abundance in 2019 at
87.8 billion fish, compared with 81.1 billion in the accepted 2024 assessment, a revision
of 8.3%. The revision reflected both updated observations and changes in model
structure.

The estimate for the same 2024 female spawning biomass changed from 3.389 million t in the saved
2024 assessment to 3.526 million t in Model 26.0, a revision of 4.0%. Within the trajectory,
spawning biomass changed from that 2024 estimate to 3.057 million t in 2026 (-13.3%). Total
biomass changed from 10.767 million t to 12.162 million t over the same years (13.0%).
These within-trajectory changes differed from shared-year assessment revisions.

[Figure 33](#fig-recruitment-2024-current) compared recruitment from Models 26.0 and 26.1.2
with the accepted 2024 assessment, using the calendar year each cohort entered at age 1. The two
current fits showed a similar pattern of strong and weak year classes. The 2024 series used point
estimates from the original assessment rather than the 23.0 refit with data through 2026. Error bars
for the current models were approximate 95% confidence
intervals using the fitted parameter covariance for Model 26.0 and the marginal likelihood for
Model 26.1.2.

Model 26.0 estimated higher female spawning biomass over the shared fitted years shown in
[Figure 34](#fig-projection-vintages) (2002--2024). Its Scenario 2 point projections rise in 2027
and 2028, whereas the 2024 assessment projected a decline from 2025 through 2028. Each assessment
used its own Scenario 2 catch assumptions. The Model 26.0 band reflected uncertainty in the fitted
assessment parameters under the stated projection assumptions.

#### Recruitment per unit of spawning biomass

[Figure 35](#fig-model260-lnrs) showed Model 26.0 estimates of log recruits per spawner. For each year
of hatching, age-1 recruitment in the following year was divided by female spawning biomass in the year of hatching. Taking the natural
logarithm puts proportional changes on a comparable scale: higher values indicated more recruits per
unit of spawning biomass. The series showed substantial variation among year classes. The 1978, 2008
and 2018 year classes had particularly high recruits-per-spawner values. Following the strong 2018
year class, the ratio declined through the 2022 year class; estimates for 2023--2025 were higher but
remain less certain because fewer observation years were available and the surveys and fishery
sample a smaller proportion of younger fish, especially ages 1–3, than older fish. The spawning-biomass panel generally showed lower ratios at higher biomass, with
considerable variation among years at similar biomass. This pattern can reflect density dependence,
environmental conditions and estimation uncertainty. Spawning biomass appears in both the horizontal
axis and the ratio, which can contribute to the apparent relationship. Model 26.0 used mean
recruitment rather than a fitted stock–recruitment relationship. The figure provided a descriptive check on
productivity using point estimates of the recruitment-to-biomass ratio.

Biological schedules and selectivity were shown by age, sex and year
([Figure 36](#fig-model262-current-biological-schedules);
[Table 36](#tbl-model262-current-biological-schedules);
[Table 37](#tbl-model262-current-selectivity)). Fishing mortality was also shown by age
([Figure 37](#fig-model260-fishing-mortality-age)). Whole-year spawning exploitation compared paired
spawning-biomass calculations from the base case model production fit
([Figure 38](#fig-model260-spawn-interval-exploitation)). Spawning exploitation was the percentage
reduction in next-spawning female biomass caused by fishing: 100 × (1 − biomass with fishing /
biomass without fishing). For the interval from spawning in 2026 to spawning in 2027, its
production-point estimate was 13.7%: 3.326 million t with fishing
versus 3.853 million t without fishing. The branches share prior fishing history and their
spawning-date starting population, with 1.375 million t annual catch assumed in 2027. The separate
MCMC posterior median for this exploitation fraction was 14.5%, with a central 95% credible
interval of 11.2--18.4%. These paired-state calculations carry the revised fishery-weight
schedule into 2027 and retained the fixed 1.375 million t catch assumption. The production-fit point
remained separate from that posterior interval.

### 6.1.2 Estimated and fixed model parameters

Fixed parameters are shown in [Section 4.3](#sec-other-data) while [Table 38](#tbl-model262-current-parameter-families) gives the minimum and maximum estimates and
the median and maximum asymptotic standard errors for each parameter group, including three log
catchability estimates and 63 recruitment deviations. Complete estimates and the largest parameter
correlations were retained in [the detailed estimates appendix](#sec-current-output-appendix). The
summary likelihood contributions were in [Table 39](#tbl-model262-current-likelihood-summary).

### 6.1.3 Fits to the observations

The fitted biomass indices generally follow broad survey trends, including the low ATS
biomass in 2006--2009 and its subsequent increase ([Figure 39](#fig-model262-index-fits)). Annual
departures remained. The BTS residuals included negative departures in 2006 and 2009 and positive
departures in 2014--2015, each outside the plotted 95% reference range. The AVO observation in 2015
was also higher than fitted, whereas all ATS biomass residuals fall within that range
([Figure 40](#fig-model262-index-residuals); [Table 40](#tbl-model262-index-residual-summary)).
Thus, the broad survey trends were represented more closely than some individual annual observations.
BTS residuals account for covariance among survey years.

Fishery selectivity varied among years, with dome-shaped curves in many years and flatter curves
at older ages in others ([Figure 41](#fig-model260-fishery-selectivity-history)). Selectivity also
began to rise at younger ages in the early, pre-domestic years than in most later years.
BTS selectivity generally increased with
age and approached a plateau, while the ATS curve, shared with AVO, was relatively flat at older ages
([Figure 42](#fig-model260-bts-selectivity-history);
[Figure 43](#fig-model260-ats-selectivity-history)). Recruitment varied strongly among years: the
2018 year class, entering at age 1 in 2019, had the largest positive departure from the fitted
recruitment level.

The mean-age comparisons showed that the model followed most of the observed changes in survey age
composition and closely tracked fishery mean age in the domestic period. The clearest sustained
fishery discrepancy occurs in 1965–1975, when predicted mean ages were higher than observed
([Figure 44](#fig-model260-observed-predicted-mean-age)). The observed bars showed plus or minus two
standard errors of mean age; they described sampling uncertainty, rather than uncertainty in the
fitted population. Fishery age observations ended in 2025. The annual composition panels showed how
these mean ages arise from the proportions at each age and allow individual cohorts to be followed
as they aged ([Figure 45](#fig-model262-fishery-cohort-fits-1);
[Figure 46](#fig-model262-fishery-cohort-fits-2); [Figure 47](#fig-model262-bts-cohort-fits);
[Figure 48](#fig-model262-ats-cohort-fits)).

Aggregate observed and fitted age proportions agree closely, especially for the fishery, but
OSA residuals showed patterns by age and year ([Figure 49](#fig-model260-composition-osa); Stewart
and Monnahan ([2025](#ref-stewart2025osa)); Monnahan et al. ([2026](#ref-monnahan2026afscosa))). For
example, BTS residuals included extended runs of the same sign at several ages, and the early fishery
residuals also showed structured departures. Averaging across years can obscure these differences. The
OSA residual standard deviations were below one for all three sources (about 0.76 for the fishery,
0.86 for BTS and 0.64 for ATS), and the QQ plots were generally narrower than the standard-normal
reference. Some BTS tail residuals were large, and the ATS QQ plot also departs from the reference.
Close aggregate fits therefore need to be considered alongside the annual patterns. These residuals assessed observation fit conditional on the
fitted model parameters.

### 6.1.4 Profile likelihood diagnostics {#sec-model260-ats-q-profile}

A likelihood profile examined how strongly the observations and model assumptions constrain ATS survey
catchability (ATS-q) in Model 26.0. The catchability parameter scales the ATS  index relative to the population
available to the survey. We fixed this parameter at 17 values from 0.45 to 0.65, including the
freely estimated value of 0.51694, and re-estimated all other active parameters. The grid used
eight equal intervals on each side of the estimated value: approximately 0.00837 below it and
0.01663 above it ([Figure 50](#fig-model260-ats-q-profile)).

The lowest NLL for ATS-q was 0.51694. ATS-q values between  0.4576 and 0.5838 were below 1.92 NLL units.

NLL profiles by likelihood component shows that both the index and composition data inform the ATS-q parameter.

All 17 fits had maximum absolute gradients below $10^{-4}$ and positive-definite Hessians. Weighted NLL
components sum to the total objective at every point. Further evaluation could consider
sensitivity to data weighting and selectivity assumptions.

[Figure 51](#fig-model260-ats-q-marginal-profile) compared the negative log
ATS-q marginal density with its optimized NLL profile, showing very similar outcomes for the two methods. The kernel density integrated to one, and
each displayed curve was centered at its own minimum over ATS-q. The negative log marginal density integrated over the
other parameters and included posterior regularization; the profile optimizes those parameters under
the native penalized objective.The final ATS-q posterior median was 0.5093, with a central 95% credible interval of
0.4514--0.5755  Panel B fitted weighted quadratic curves directly to individual-draw
native NLL components and compared them with the profile components (the MCMC quadratic method). Here, MCMC curves were centered at the ATS-q parameter's marginal mode and displayed over the
central 99% of sampled catchability. Smoothers were used to summarize the broad component trends, with tail coverage limited by the available
draws. For the index data, both the MCMC quadratic method and the profile indicate a best value between 0.55 and 0.60 for ATS-q, while results between the two methods are not as clearly aligned for the composition data and selectivity deviates.

The paired MCMC draws show the relationships among ATS-q, summed abundance at ages 2--5 in 2026,
age-1 abundance in 2019 (the 2018 year class), and projected 2027 female spawning biomass
([Figure 52](#fig-model260-ats-bts-q-ssb2027-pairs)). Diagonal panels showed their marginal densities.
All four quantities were paired within each saved draw.

Projected 2027 female spawning biomass was most strongly associated with the summed abundance of ages
2--5 in 2026 among the quantities shown ($r = 0.84$). This contrasts sharply with the 2024
assessment, in which projected 2025 spawning biomass depended heavily on the estimated magnitude of
the 2018 year class (Figure 53 of the 2024 SAFE). The 2018 year-class dependence remained in the
projection, as shown by its positive correlation with 2027 spawning biomass ($r = 0.36$), but was
less pronounced than the dependence on the younger fish now approaching or contributing to spawning
biomass.

In [Table 41](#tbl-model260-ats-q-ssb2027), we show projected 2027 spawning biomass for a range of fixed ATS q values. These projected spawning biomass values and corresponding approximate 95% confidence intervals were based on fitting the model to the data conditioned on fixed ATS q values (with all other parameters estimated). Estimates of projected 2027 spawning biomass range from 2,968 kt with ATS q fixed at 0.65 to 3,567 kt with an ATS q fixed at 0.45.

### 6.1.5 Retrospective patterns {#sec-paired-current-retrospectives}

The retrospective analysis showed substantially smaller estimates of 2016--2019 spawning biomass and larger estimates of maximum F from the current model run, relative to those estimates from runs with data endpoint years 2017--2020 ([Figure 53](#fig-current-observed-retrospective-trajectories), [Table 43](#tbl-model260-current-retrospective-revisions)). Additionally, estimates of the 2008, 2012, and 2013 year classes become smaller with the addition of new data. Retrospective patterns for Model 26.1.2 (the sensitivity run splitting early and late fishery characteristics) were nearly identical to those from Model 26.0 (the base model). Across the full nine peels ending in 2017--2025, Mohn's rho for spawning biomass was
+0.121 ([Table 42](#tbl-catch-revised-mohn-rho)).

The Model 26.0 simulated-data and posterior-predictive retrospective experiments provided separate
conditional comparisons ([Section 6.3.1](#sec-model260-selftest)).

[Figure 54](#fig-historical-retrospectives) compared beginning-of-year age-3+ biomass from earlier
assessments with this year's base model, Model 26.0. Estimated biomass trends over time are consistent across the current and historical assessments. Historical estimates of age 3 biomass from this year's base model are larger than for the 2024 assessment in many years, but nearly identical in years of low biomass. The plot shows that in period of higher biomass, the current model estimates of age 3 biomass are largely consistent with the 2007--2023 assessment results.

### 6.1.6 Age-composition weighting comparison {#sec-francis-comparison}

We compared the sample sizes used in the 2026 models to those calculated from the approach described in Francis (2011), showing that for the fishery and BTS age composition data, the two approaches to data weighting lead to very similar resulting sample sizes;  [Figure 55](#fig-francis-sample-size-comparison);
[Figure 56](#fig-francis-mean-age-residuals)).

## 6.2 Model 26.1 split-fishery alternatives {#sec-model261-results}

Models 26.1.0 and 26.1.1 separated the Foreign fishery through 1990 from the Modern domestic fishery
beginning in 1991. Their annual selectivity standard deviations were fixed at 0.5, while the
declining-age penalty was 12.5 in Model 26.1.0 and 3.125 in Model 26.1.1. The zero-penalty case
provided a further comparison. The Model 26.1.2 sensitivity shown here retained the 3.125 penalty and
fixed the Foreign and Modern annual process standard deviations at 0.1235 and 0.582, respectively.
The remaining parameters and annual selectivity effects were estimated conditionally on these values.

The likelihood comparison separated data-likelihood contributions, penalty terms and the marginal
fitting criterion ([Table 44](#tbl-model261-nll-comparison)). The projections used the revised
ordinary fits and the Early-late fishery split Model 26.1.2 comparison. The alternatives retained
matched observations, likelihood weights and projection assumptions
([Table 45](#tbl-coordinated-model-abc)).

### 6.2.1 Selectivity

Separating the Foreign (1964--1990) and Modern domestic (1991--2026) fisheries changed the fitted
selectivity most visibly near the boundary between the two periods. Over much of the later period,
Models 26.0 and 26.1.0 retained similar annual age patterns, including the peaks and declines at older
ages ([Figure 57](#fig-model261-selectivity-history)). The split allowed the Foreign curve to differ
more freely from the Modern curve, while Model 26.0 represented the history as a single fishery.

Both models estimated a shift from 1990 to 1991 toward lower relative selectivity at younger ages and
higher relative selectivity at ages 11 and older. The shift was larger in Model 26.1.0: at age 5, the
change was about −0.69 on the native mean-one scale, compared with −0.31 in Model 26.0; at ages 12
and older, the increases were about 0.55 and 0.24, respectively
([Figure 58](#fig-model261-selectivity-boundary)). This comparison showed how the split changed the
