estimated transition. The fitted curves alone established neither an abrupt change in fishing
practices nor an improvement in the population estimates; the observation fits and retrospective
results provided the complementary checks below.

The full-history curves were divided by each year's maximum so that their shapes can be compared. The
boundary-year display instead retained native mean-one normalization, and its differences referred to
that scale. These were fitted point curves. The Model 26.1.2 curves used in subsequent comparisons
retained the fitted selectivity states from its fixed-SD conditional fit and remained distinct from the
Model 26.1.0 comparison here.

### 6.2.2 Fishery age-composition fits {#sec-fishery-composition-comparison}

We compared Models 26.0 and 26.1.2 using the same 62 annual fishery age compositions and likelihood
weights ([Figure 59](#fig-model260-fishery-fit-comparison);
[Figure 60](#fig-model2612-fishery-fit-comparison)). Model 26.0 fitted one fishery across the full
record; Model 26.1.2 separated the Foreign fishery through 1990 from the Modern domestic fishery
beginning in 1991. We displayed both models over those same periods to compare their fits directly.
Both models reproduced the dominant age groups in the combined compositions, while the annual plots
revealed differences that the combined summaries obscured.

Model 26.1.2 fitted the Modern domestic observations more closely. It reduced the sample-weighted
root-mean-square difference in age proportions from 0.693 to 0.590 percentage points and the
root-mean-square error in annual mean age from 0.123 to 0.0963 years. Both models predicted a
younger mean age than the observations showed in 1991, but Model 26.1.2 reduced that discrepancy
from 0.510 to 0.339 years. The smaller differences across ages and years showed that the
split-fishery configuration improved the modern fit rather than simply matching its combined age
distribution.

Model 26.0 fitted the Foreign-period observations more closely. Model 26.1.2 increased the
sample-weighted age-proportion error from 2.67 to 3.43 percentage points and the annual mean-age
error from 0.655 to 0.696 years. Both models predicted older mean ages than the early
observations showed, particularly in 1964--1965 and 1970. The age-by-year panels showed persistent
overprediction at several older ages and underprediction at younger ages during much of the early
record. Separating the fisheries therefore improved the modern fit while leaving larger
discrepancies in the Foreign period.

## 6.3 Further model evaluations {#sec-evaluation}

### 6.3.1 Observation-error retrospective self-test {#sec-model260-selftest}

In response to Plan Team and SSC requests to investigate retrospective patterns, we developed a new
simulation-based retrospective experiment for this assessment
([Figure 61](#fig-current-simulation-retrospective-revisions)). Its distinctive feature was a paired
design that examined revisions both at the fitted parameter estimates and across plausible parameter
states from the regularized posterior. One set of ten simulated datasets used the fitted parameters;
a second set used ten posterior parameter draws. Each dataset had its own full 2026 fit and nine
optimization peels ending in 2017--2025. Revisions compared each peel's terminal estimate with its
own full fit for the same calendar year. This approach extended the usual retrospective analysis by
examining how observation variation and uncertainty in the generating parameters influenced the
revisions, providing additional context for interpreting the assessment's retrospective pattern.

Across all nine peels ending in 2017--2025, Model 26.0 assessment Mohn's rho for female spawning
biomass was +0.121, compared with median values of −0.0117 for datasets generated at the
fitted parameters and −0.0574 for datasets generated from posterior draws. The assessment value
exceeded every simulated rho in both sets: the fixed-parameter range was −0.115 to +0.0335, and
the posterior-draw range was −0.0971 to +0.116. Thus, the positive average spawning-biomass
revision in the assessment was stronger than that reproduced by these simulated datasets.

For age-1 recruitment, the assessment's nine-peel rho was −0.0985, within both simulated ranges.
Median recruitment rho was −0.00751 in the fixed-parameter set and +0.0830 in the
posterior-draw set. The contrast between spawning biomass and recruitment showed that the
retrospective pattern depended on the population quantity considered.

The paired design explored how observation variation and uncertainty in generating parameters
contributed to the full nine-peel pattern. Ten datasets per branch provided an exploratory comparison.
The technical supplement described the fixed process history, data-generation approximations and
other conditioning assumptions. These experiments assessed biomass and recruitment revisions.
Confidence bands describing retrospective ABC or OFL patterns were beyond the scope of this work but
would be interesting to evaluate.

### 6.3.2 Posterior diagnostics and predictive checks {#sec-model260-posterior-review}

The regularized posterior explored parameter uncertainty separately from the production base case model
estimates ([Figure 62](#fig-model260-snuts-pairs); [Figure 63](#fig-model260-snuts-uncertainty);
[Figure 64](#fig-model260-snuts-marginals)). Four chains each retained 1,250 draws after 1,000
warmup iterations. Combined parameter diagnostics gave maximum R-hat 1.024 and minimum bulk ESS 242,
with zero divergences and zero maximum-treedepth events. The reported population quantities mixed more
consistently: maximum R-hat was 1.0013 and minimum bulk ESS was 3,914. MCMC standard errors of the
2026 spawning-biomass and biomass means were about 4,110 t and 20,600 t; their first-half versus
second-half mean shifts were less than 0.03 posterior standard deviations. These diagnostics described
the saved chains and retained the parameter-level qualifications.

#### Posterior summaries

The posterior mean female spawning biomass in 2026 was 2.965 million t, with a central 95% credible
interval of 2.450--3.584 million t ([Table 46](#tbl-catch-revised-posterior-check)). These summaries used all 5,000 retained MCMC draws under the regularizing priors and fixed biological inputs.
Full-precision results were downloadable as CSV files containing terminal stock and selectivity
summaries (CSV), annual population intervals (CSV), summaries of all 1,266 parameters (CSV), and
spawning-exploitation intervals (CSV).

Predictive checks asked whether the fitted model can generate data that resemble the observations
([Figure 65](#fig-model260-index-ppc); [Figure 66](#fig-model260-composition-ppc)). We selected
1,000 MCMC draws spanning the four chains. Each draw supplied a possible set of model parameters,
from which a new set of observations was simulated. The shaded ranges therefore included both
parameter uncertainty and the sampling variation assumed by the model. Points outside these ranges,
or repeated patterns of differences, helped identify features the model struggled to reproduce. The
ranges applied to each age or year individually; some points outside them were expected even when the
assumptions were appropriate.

For the indices, simulated observations used the same error assumptions used in fitting, including
the relationships among BTS errors. The overall BTS mismatch measure was as large as the observed
measure in only 0.2% of the simulations, indicating that this feature of the BTS data was rarely
reproduced. Normal error assumptions also allow some simulated indices to be negative.

For age compositions, simulated fish were randomly assigned to age groups using each draw's predicted
proportions and the sample size used in fitting, rounded to a whole number. The simulations
approximate the fitting method, which added a small constant (0.001) to age proportions. The figure
compared the latest three actual samples for each source with these simulated age proportions. Age
conversions, weights and other biological inputs were held fixed. These checks assess how well the
model reproduced observations; the retrospective analyses addressed how estimates changed as additional
years of data become available.

# 7 Projections and harvest recommendations {#sec-projections}

## 7.1 Proposed Tier 3 configuration and reference points

The proposed fishery selectivity was the mean of the 2023--2025 annual curves, the latest three years
with fishery age observations. Each age was averaged before scaling the resulting curve to an arithmetic mean
of one over ages 1--14 and 15+, consistent with earlier assessments. The separately inferred 2026 curve was distinguished from directly age-informed years ([the
projection-input appendix](#sec-proposed-projection-input-curves)).

The deterministic recruitment level used the arithmetic mean of age-1 entries in 1978--2023,
corresponding to birth cohorts 1977--2022. The less precise 2024--2026 entries were excluded. Every
entry in the advice tables equaled this selected historical mean. The separate projection figures added
future recruitment variation to illustrate a range of possible paths. Reference points and fishing
rates were reported in [Table 47](#tbl-proposed-tier3-reference-points). The Model 26.1.2 column used
the revised Early-late fishery split comparison under the same projection assumptions.

The Tier 3 reference points were spawning-potential quantities. The ABC rule reduced fishing
mortality below B40% and sets it to zero below B20%. Projections start from each fitted population
and used the stated catch scenarios and biological inputs. The author-rate fraction was one, subject
to the risk evaluation and final review.

The previous-year OFL-equivalent fishing mortality was reported in [Section 10](#sec-prior-year-ofl-f).

## 7.2 Standard harvest scenarios

The proposed projections retained the standard harvest scenarios and their common biology
([Table 48](#tbl-proposed-tier3-scenarios)). The expected-catch scenario assumed 1.375 million t in
each of 2027 and 2028; the 2028 catch was a planning assumption. Short-term outputs were reported in
[Table 49](#tbl-proposed-tier3-short-term).

The catch and female spawning-biomass panels compared Alternative 2 with recent-mean-F Alternative 3
([Figure 67](#fig-proposed-tier3-catch); [Figure 68](#fig-proposed-tier3-ssb)). Black lines showed the
means of 1,000 future-recruitment simulations, ribbons showed their 5th--95th percentiles, and ten
colored trajectories illustrate individual outcomes. Each color followed the same recruitment
realization across both alternatives and figures. Recruitment followed the established
inverse-Gaussian method, using the arithmetic and harmonic means of the fitted 1978--2023 age-1
entries. Initial age-1 abundance in 2027 equals the historical arithmetic mean; each subsequent
entry varied among simulations. The widening bands showed how future recruitment variation accumulated
as new cohorts enter the fishery and spawning population. Alternative 2 catch paths coincide in 2027
and 2028 because those catches were prescribed.

The projection tables retained all seven scenarios with recruitment fixed at the historical arithmetic
mean ([Table 50](#tbl-proposed-tier3-catch); [Table 51](#tbl-proposed-tier3-ssb); [Table
52](#tbl-proposed-tier3-f)). The historical phase plot places the fitted 1981--2026 trajectory and
deterministic Alternative 2 projections for 2027--2028 on common axes ([Figure
69](#fig-proposed-tier3-phase)). The horizontal axis was female spawning biomass divided by B35%; the
vertical axis was mean fishing mortality across model ages divided by F35%. Both denominators were the current
primary projection reference points (B35% = 2.155 million t; F35% = 0.429 per year), held constant
across the trajectory. This common benchmark showed changes in the fitted stock and fishing mortality
through time. The 2024 assessment used annually varying reference points; the historical positions
here therefore also reflect the choice of a common current benchmark. F35% was a spawning-per-recruit
proxy for FMSY, and B35% was the corresponding spawning-biomass reference point. Solid lines mark
ratios of one, and the dashed vertical line marks half B35%. Two-digit year labels trace the
trajectory, with the two projection years boxed and shaded yellow. The fitted 2026 position and both
projected positions were above B35% and below F35%.

### 7.2.1 Decision table {#sec-catch-decision-probabilities}

As in past assessments, we present estimated consequences and probabilities for a range of future
catches and the subsequent fishing effort implied by each choice
([Table 53](#tbl-current-decision-definitions); [Table 54](#tbl-current-decision-model26)). The
decision table compared eight possible 2027 catches, from 10 to 2,540 kt, using Model 26.0 with the
updated AVO data. The indicator definitions identify the quantities, comparison benchmarks and years
used in the calculations. Together, the tables showed how catch choices affected fishing mortality,
future spawning biomass and age structure, and how likely each choice was to meet the specified
benchmarks.

Each catch column represented a different fishing strategy. Fishing mortality was calculated to
achieve that catch in 2027, then held constant through 2031. Catches in subsequent years therefore
change with the projected abundance and age composition of the stock. The effort indicator gave the
probability that mean age-specific fishing mortality in 2027 exceeds its 2026 value. Interpreting it
as relative effort assumed that catchability and the age pattern of fishery selectivity remain
fixed. It provided a comparison among strategies rather than a forecast of vessel numbers, fishing
days or operating costs.

Readers can compare columns to examine the trade-off between the initial catch and subsequent stock
conditions. The probability rows summarize the chance of crossing the stated biomass,
fishing-mortality or age-structure benchmarks. These were conditional comparisons that supported catch
decisions alongside the standard harvest projections and risk table.

Entries were approximate chances out of 100. They propagate uncertainty in the fitted population,
selectivity, estimated mean recruitment and comparison benchmarks. Future recruitment was held at the
estimated 1978--2023 mean, and biological schedules were fixed. These probabilities described
uncertainty in the assessment estimates under each catch choice. Additional year-to-year recruitment
variation and uncertainty in weights and maturity were outside these calculations. Values displayed
as 0 or 100 reflected rounding.

The 1,270-kt column was retained for comparison with the earlier decision-table analysis. The
expected-catch scenario elsewhere in this section assumed 1,375 kt in 2027 and 2028. The decision
tables provided a broader comparison of catch choices; they used local asymptotic uncertainty rather
than MCMC draws.

### 7.2.2 Reference point sensitivity to fishery selectivity specification {#sec-projection-selectivity-sensitivity}

Fishery selectivity determined how fishing mortality was distributed across ages and therefore
affects both the reference fishing rates and the catches obtained at those rates. The central
projection used the age-specific arithmetic mean of the raw 2023--2025 fishery selectivity curves,
rescaled so that its mean over ages 1--14 and 15+ was one. This recent three-year average smooths annual variation while
retaining the age pattern from the latest years with fishery age observations. Averaging precedes
rescaling because normalizing each annual curve first would give a different average.
[Figure 70](#fig-projection-selectivity-recent) introduces this recent-average specification and
contrasts it with individual annual estimates. The inferred 2026 curve was shown separately because
fishery age observations end in 2025. It provided a terminal-year comparison, while the management
projections retained the 2023--2025 average.

The recent curves showed that changes in fishery recruitment involve particular ages rather than a
uniform shift toward younger fish. The first ascending half-maximum crossing was near age 6 in
2021--2022, compared with approximately 4.5, 5.0 and 5.2 in 2023--2025. Relative selectivity at age
5 was especially high in 2023 and then declined in 2024--2025. Selectivity at ages 1--3 remained low
and varied independently. These differences matter because a curve that exposes age-5 fish more
strongly can produce a different catch and spawning impact from one that concentrates fishing at
older ages, even when both had the same maximum selectivity.

The full annual comparisons showed which parts of each curve differ from the projection assumption
([Figure 71](#fig-projection-selectivity-annual)). The repeated 2023--2025 reference makes shifts in
the ascending limb, peak and older-age tail visible across 2007--2026. For example, the 2019 curve
peaks near age 7 and declines substantially at older ages, whereas several earlier curves retained
high selectivity across the older ages. Thus, the annual panels provided the age-specific explanation
for the management differences in the next figure. The older curves represented alternative fishing
patterns for sensitivity analysis. Their relevance as forecasts depended on evidence about current
and future fishery conditions.

Annual selectivity alternatives give both higher and lower catch ceilings than the recent-average
baseline ([Figure 72](#fig-projection-selectivity-effects)). Of the twenty curves, 14 produce a
higher maximum ABC in 2027 and 12 do so in 2028. Changes range from -8.2% to +12.0% in 2027 and from
-5.9% to +8.4% in 2028. These were conditional sensitivities under common population, recruitment,
biological and catch assumptions.

The lowest annual-curve maximum ABC occurred with the 2018 curve in 2027 and the 2019 curve in 2028.
The 2025 curve changed the ceilings by +1.5% and -4.4%, respectively. The age pattern affected
immediate catches and the ages surviving into the following year. F40% and F35% were recalculated for
each curve; the assumed catch remained 1.375 million t in each year.

The younger-age summaries explain why a single description such as "younger selection" was
insufficient ([Figure 73](#fig-projection-selectivity-trends)). They separated exposure of ages 1--3,
selectivity at ages 4 and 5, the first ascending half-maximum age, and changes across the full
curve. For example, from 2022 to 2023 the half-maximum age fell from about 6.0 to 4.5 years, while
the curve-weighted mean age changed only from 10.09 to 10.00 years. Conversely, from 2023 to 2025
the half-maximum age rose while the curve-weighted mean age fell. The ascending limb and older-age
tail therefore move in different directions. This figure connected the detailed annual panels to the
reference-point results: the age at which fish begin entering the fishery and the relative exposure
of older fish carry different information. Its mean-age measure weights selectivity equally across
model ages 1--15, with age 15 representing the plus group; population abundance and catch
composition were excluded from that shape index.

The reference-rate comparison makes the dependence on age selection explicit
([Figure 74](#fig-selectivity-f35-mean-age)). Under fixed biology, each curve had its own
F35% rate under mean-one selectivity, the fishing-mortality scalar that reduced lifetime spawning output per recruit
to 35% of the unfished level. Later exposure can allow more spawning before capture and therefore
support a higher reference rate at the same spawning-per-recruit target. However, the full
curve, including its older-age tail, determined this response. The high 2019 F35% illustrates how a
reference scalar can rise sharply under a particular age pattern. Such an increase described the
rate permitted under that pattern; it provided no independent evidence of increased stock
productivity or a larger sustainable catch.

Two distinctions were essential when interpreting an FMSY proxy against selected age. First, F35% was
a spawning-per-recruit proxy for FMSY, whereas FMSY itself depended on the equilibrium yield and
recruitment relationship. The historical FMSY comparison and this F35% diagnostic therefore
represented different reference quantities. Second, F was a scalar: fishing mortality at
each age equals that scalar multiplied by selectivity at that age. Comparisons among years require
the same selectivity normalization and the corresponding age-specific mortality pattern. The
scatterplot used a selectivity-weighted age index over ages 1--10, whereas its spawning-per-recruit
calculation included ages 1--14 and 15+, fixed natural mortality, maturity and the selected
projection spawning weights, and quarter-year spawning timing. Its age index also differed from the
ages 1--15 index in the preceding figure and from the abundance-weighted age of selected fish. It was
a compact descriptor of curve shape, and a common mean selected age can accompany different
reference rates. The complete selectivity curve and resulting catch and spawning effects provided the
appropriate basis for interpreting the FMSY proxy and comparing harvest specifications.

# 8 Risk table and ABC recommendation {#sec-risk-table-abc}

The author risk evaluation retained all four categories at **Level 1 -- Normal**
([Table 55](#tbl-risk-summary)). The ecosystem and fishery observations were summarized below.
Working recommendations remain subject to author scientific evaluation and Plan Team, SSC and
Council review. The Level 1 evaluation supported no reduction from maximum permissible ABC.

::: {#tbl-risk-summary .report-table .unnumbered data-table="tables/004-tbl-risk-summary.csv"}

Table 55: 2026 risk-category scores and supporting summaries. Assessment-related and
fishery-informed stock evaluations were **Level 1 -- Normal**; population dynamics and ecosystem
evaluations draw on the synthesis by Elizabeth Siddon and Kalei Shotwell.

:::

## 8.1 Assessment-related considerations {#sec-risk-assessment}

Model 26.0 (Rceattle) was the adopted assessment model and main proposal for Tier 3 calculations and
specifications. The alternative models examined how the assessment responded to changes in its
structure and treatment of annual selectivity variation. Comparisons with Models 23.0 and 23.2
connect the current assessment to the previous formulation and help distinguish the effects of
updated observations from changes in model structure. The split-fishery alternatives test whether
separate selectivity patterns for the Foreign fishery in 1964--1990 and the Modern domestic fishery
from 1991 onward better represent the fishing history. Further comparisons varied the constraint on
declining selectivity and the treatment of year-to-year changes in selectivity.

Model 26.1.2 provided the principal sensitivity to these choices. Its underlying marginal
formulation estimated the variability of Modern fishery selectivity while accounting for annual
selectivity effects. The conditional comparison presented here fixed the Foreign and Modern process
standard deviations at their selected full-data values and estimated the remaining parameters and
annual selectivity effects. This configuration fitted the Modern fishery age compositions more closely
than Model 26.0, while larger discrepancies remain in the Foreign period. The result identified a
potential benefit of separating the fisheries, alongside a trade-off in how the model represented the
earlier observations.

The Model 26.1.2 retrospective analysis asked whether estimates changed as the most recent
observations were successively removed. Each shortened-data fit holds the process standard deviations
fixed and was compared with a full-data fit using the same conditional estimation method. This
matching reference makes the retrospective differences interpretable within the fixed-SD
configuration. The diagnostic therefore described stability when the assumed magnitude of annual
selectivity variation was held constant. Re-estimating that variation in each shortened dataset could
change the retrospective pattern, and uncertainty in the process standard deviations remained outside
this comparison. Improved fits to the Modern observations consequently provided one part of the model
evaluation; broader retrospective reliability required evidence across the relevant estimation
choices. Model 26.0 remained the basis for the Tier 3 specifications, with Model 26.1.2 used to
assess sensitivity to fishery structure and selectivity assumptions.

## 8.2 Population dynamics risk summary

Population dynamics risk was **Level 1 -- Normal**. Cold spring conditions coincided with low egg and
larval abundance; temperature-dependent timing complicates interpretation of these early-life
indices. Southeastern Bering Sea (SEBS) age-0 abundance was also low. Above-average late-summer
large copepod abundance, lipid-rich copepods and euphausiids, and above-average SEBS age-0 energy
density indicate favorable feeding and potential survival through the first winter. Northern Bering
Sea (NBS) age-0 energy density was below average, while adult-pollock cannibalism was low overall;
age-1 specificity remained unverified. The regional contrasts and supporting evidence were described
in [Section 11.1](#sec-ecosystem-population-dynamics) within
[Section 11](#sec-ecosystem-considerations).

## 8.3 Environmental and ecosystem risk summary

The environmental and ecosystem synthesis supported a **Level 1 -- Normal** ecosystem score.
Following the warm period of 2014--2021 and near-average thermal conditions in 2022--2025, the EBS
shelf shifted to cool conditions in 2026. The expanded cold pool, abundant lipid-rich prey and
improving adult condition provide favorable context for juvenile and adult pollock. Increased
pollock biomass may increase competition; prey and condition indicators suggested adequate food, while
the effects of increasing sablefish abundance remain a research question.
[Section 11](#sec-ecosystem-considerations) presents the detailed distribution, environmental, prey,
competitor and predator evidence, including conditions for later juveniles and adults in
[Section 11.2](#sec-ecosystem-juveniles-adults). These category scores supported the recommendation
for no reduction from maximum permissible ABC.

## 8.4 Fishery-informed Stock Considerations {#sec-risk-fishery}

Fishing conditions differed between the two seasons. The observer data indicated that A-season
fishing in 2026 appeared good. Later in the B-season, fishing occurred farther north than normal,
and pollock of desirable sizes were limited. The late-season observations therefore qualify the
favorable A-season picture and identify changes in where fishing occurred and the sizes available to
the fishery.

We retained the **Level 1 -- Normal** score for fishery-informed stock considerations. This score
reflected the author's qualitative assessment of fishing conditions across the year. The observations provided context for interpreting fishery performance; their implications for stock-wide abundance
remain uncertain. A standardized comparison of fishing locations, effort and size composition would
help distinguish changes in fishery availability from changes in overall stock abundance.

## 8.5 Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile development

Development of the EBS pollock Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile (ESP) continued alongside the
assessment ([Shotwell et al. 2026](#ref-shotwell2026pollockesp)). The archived September 2026
development report supplied exploratory background, and the AI-assisted draft appeared as [Appendix
B](#sec-esp-2026-appendix). The 2026 Eastern Bering Sea Ecosystem Status Report described an
external Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling (DSEM) analysis that identified sea ice extent,
sea surface temperature (SST) and summer large copepods as indicators with statistically
supported relationships to age-1 recruitment ([Siddon 2026](#ref-siddon2026ebs)). The exploratory
Rceattle DSEM pilot in the appendix used late-summer SST and cold-pool extent as two environmental
proxies. Its scope supported a separate assessment of those proxies. Evaluating all three external
relationships within Rceattle required additional testing.

The first application of DSEM was completed as a draft in the [ESP
draft](#sec-esp-2026-appendix). Development and implementation of an integrated version within
Rceattle continue from the work presented in the September 2026 development document ([Ianelli et
al. 2026](#ref-ianelli2026developments)). We see the Ecosystem Status Report (ESR), the ESP, and
integration of ecosystem information within the full assessment model as logical applications of
ecosystem-based methods for providing informed catch advice to the Council.

Since all four categories are **Level 1 -- Normal**, we recommend no reduction from maximum permissible ABC.

# 9 Status determination {#sec-status-determination}

Under the Magnuson--Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, stock status is evaluated for
overfishing, an overfished condition, and the risk of approaching an overfished condition.

For Tier 3, B35% is the BMSY proxy. MSST is evaluated using the biomass and projection tests below.
Alternative 6 fishes at the OFL rate in every projected year. Alternative 7 fishes at the
maximum-ABC rate in 2027--2028 and the OFL rate from 2029 onward.

Overfishing in 2025. Catch of 1,326,215.61 t was below the specified Bering Sea subarea OFL of
2,957,000 t. Thus, the stock was not subjected to overfishing in 2025.

Overfished in 2026. Biomass below half B35% indicated an overfished condition; biomass above B35%
indicated the stock was above MSST. Between those levels, status depended on Alternative 6 biomass in
2036: below B35% indicated an overfished condition; otherwise, the stock was above MSST. Current
biomass was 3.057 million t for Model 26.0 and 3.065 million t for the Early-late fishery split Model
26.1.2 sensitivity, above their respective B35% values of 2.155 and 2.177 million t. Both therefore
indicated the stock was not overfished; the 2036 test was unnecessary.

Approaching an overfished condition. Under Alternative 7, 2028 biomass below half B35% indicated an
approaching overfished condition; biomass above B35% indicated it was not approaching that condition.
If that biomass fell between half B35% and B35%, use Alternative 7 biomass in 2038 for the
long-term test. Biomass below B35% in that long-term test indicated an approaching overfished
condition. Projected 2028 biomass was 3.123 million t for Model 26.0 and 3.179 million t for Model
26.1.2, both above B35%. Neither model indicated an approaching overfished condition; the 2038 test
was unnecessary.

These comparisons used deterministic historical-mean recruitment. Assessment conclusions and adopted
catch specifications remained separate from final NMFS status determinations.

::: {#status-model-options .report-table .unnumbered data-table="tables/005-status-model-options.csv"}

:::

# 10 F limit {#sec-prior-year-ofl-f}

Following section 4.15 of the assessment guidelines, F limit was reverse-engineered as the annual
fishing mortality that would have produced the previous year's OFL using the recommended model's
estimated population for that year. For this 2026 assessment, the calculation therefore used the
adopted 2025 Bering Sea pollock OFL of 2.957 million t (National Marine Fisheries Service
([2025](#ref-noaa2025bsaifinalspecs))) and the Model 26.0 beginning-of-year 2025 numbers at age,
fishery weights, natural mortality and realized selectivity.

Solving the annual Baranov catch equation gave F limit = 0.439 per year under mean-one
selectivity, reproducing the adopted 2025 OFL. This calculation holds the fitted population and
biological inputs fixed while changing fishing mortality.

The calculation finds the value of $F_{\mathrm{limit}}$ satisfying

$$
C^{\mathrm{OFL}}_{2025}=
\sum_{a=1}^{15+} N_{a,2025}\,w^{\mathrm{fishery}}_{a,2025}
\frac{F_{\mathrm{limit}}\,s^{*}_{a,2025}}
{M_{a,2025}+F_{\mathrm{limit}}\,s^{*}_{a,2025}}
\left[1-\exp\!\left\{-\left(M_{a,2025}+F_{\mathrm{limit}}\,s^{*}_{a,2025}\right)\right\}\right].
 \qquad(1)
$$

Here $N$ is beginning-of-year abundance, $w^{\mathrm{fishery}}$ is fishery weight-at-age, $M$ is
annual natural mortality, and $s^{*}$ is the fitted selectivity curve rescaled to a mean of one
over ages 1--14 and 15+. Thus $F_{\mathrm{limit}}$ is mean annual fishing mortality across model ages. Abundance in millions of fish and weight in kg give catch in thousand tons.

# 11 Ecosystem considerations {#sec-ecosystem-considerations}

A draft Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile (ESP) was presented in [Appendix
B](#sec-esp-2026-appendix). It brings together indicators of pollock habitat, food-web conditions
and fishery performance to provide context for the assessment. The ESP complemented the population
model by organizing evidence about processes that can affect year-class strength, fish growth and
the distribution of fish available to surveys and the fishery. This broader perspective helped
interpret changes in abundance and age composition alongside the environmental conditions
experienced by successive cohorts.

The draft 2026 Eastern Bering Sea Ecosystem Status Report provided the environmental and food-web
evidence summarized here ([Siddon 2026](#ref-siddon2026ebs)). In 2026, cool spring conditions and an
extensive cold pool coincided with low egg, larval and southeastern Bering Sea age-0 abundance. At
the same time, favorable zooplankton abundance and lipid content, together with above-average
southeastern Bering Sea age-0 energy density, indicated good feeding conditions for surviving
juveniles. These contrasting signals emphasize the importance of timing, region and life stage: low
early abundance and favorable later feeding conditions can occur within the same year. Their
implications for recruitment depend on survival through the subsequent winter and later juvenile
stages.

The following subsections connect these observations to pollock population processes. The first
considers environmental conditions, prey, competitors and predators affecting eggs, larvae and early
juveniles. The second addresses the distribution, feeding conditions and condition of later
juveniles and adults, including how temperature and vertical habitat use can affect survey
availability. Together, these indicators helped distinguish changes in population abundance from
changes in where fish occur and how effectively surveys sample them. The synthesis informs
interpretation of the assessment and the risk-category evaluation summarized in
[Section 8](#sec-risk-table-abc); the individual indicators provided complementary evidence rather
than a direct forecast of recruitment or an automatic adjustment to catch advice.

## 11.1 Ecosystem impacts of EBS pollock population dynamics {#sec-ecosystem-population-dynamics}

### Environmental Processes

A very weak winter Aleutian Low in 2025/2026 brought cool Arctic air across the EBS ([Lemagie and
Wang 2026](#ref-lemagiewang2026atmosphere)). Sea ice extent remained above average for six weeks
during March--April 2026 ([Thoman 2026](#ref-thoman2026seaice)). The resulting 2°C cold pool was
approximately 150% larger than in 2025 and the fifth-largest during 1982--2026; the 0°C cold pool
was the largest since 2013 ([Rohan and Barnett 2026](#ref-rohanbarnett2026coldpool)). Sea surface
temperatures in the SEBS were colder than in 2025, especially during January--April, and remained
below average for most of the year ([Lemagie and Callahan 2026](#ref-lemagiecallahan2026sst)). In
May 2026, spring winds favored Ekman transport off the shelf, influencing larval dispersal
trajectories ([Hennon 2026](#ref-hennon2026transport)).

### Prey

Large diatom anomalies were above average during 2023--2025 ([Ostle and Batten
2026](#ref-ostlebatten2026diatoms)), and spring 2026 chlorophyll-a concentrations were average to
high across the NBS and SEBS ([Gann et al. 2026](#ref-gannetal2026chlorophyll)). These records suggested favorable prey-production conditions in their respective periods. Increased surface
phosphate and a deeper mixed layer in 2024 imply wind mixing, larger phytoplankton cells, shorter
food chains and more efficient energy transfer to juvenile fish ([Gann
2026](#ref-gann2026nutrients)).

The spring Rapid Zooplankton Assessment indicated adequate small copepod abundance, with
above-average large copepod abundance by late summer ([Kimmel et al.
2026](#ref-kimmel2026zooplankton)). Euphausiid abundance increased from 2025 ([Levine et al.
2026](#ref-levine2026euphausiids); [Spear et al. 2026](#ref-spear2026euphausiids)). Copepod and
euphausiid lipid content in the SEBS were both above average in 2026, indicating good prey quality
for pelagic juveniles ([Pinger et al. 2026](#ref-pinger2026lipids)).

Spring larval abundance and egg numbers were low, as was the larval condition ratio. Such
observations were typical of cold spring conditions over the shelf, and temperature-dependent
seasonal timing complicates their interpretation ([Siddon 2026](#ref-siddon2026ebs)). SEBS age-0
abundance was low ([Andrews, Domke, Murphy, Spear, et al. 2026](#ref-andrews2026juvenileforage)),
and age-0 energy density was above average ([Page et al. 2026](#ref-page2026juvenileenergy)). The
suggested increase in age-1 abundance in this juvenile-survey comparison remained unverified.
Length--weight residuals for small pollock (100--250 mm) in the EBS survey improved to just below
the long-term mean ([Prohaska and Rohan 2026](#ref-prohaskarohan2026condition)). In the NBS, age-0
abundance was average ([Andrews, Domke, Murphy, Spear, et al. 2026](#ref-andrews2026juvenileforage))
and energy density was below average ([Page et al. 2026](#ref-page2026juvenileenergy)).

### Competitors

Pelagic forager biomass increased from 2025 to 2026 to above its long-term mean, largely driven by a
58% increase in pollock biomass ([Siddon 2026, 7--9](#ref-siddon2026ebs)). Above-average zooplankton
quantity and quality moderate concerns about competition for prey among young pollock. SEBS
jellyfish biomass remained average ([Buser 2026](#ref-buser2026jellyfish)) to below average ([Domke
et al. 2026](#ref-domke2026jellyfish)). NBS jellyfish biomass continued its slow decline since 2023
and remained just above the time-series mean ([Domke et al. 2026](#ref-domke2026jellyfish)).

Pacific herring and capelin biomass were below average in both the NBS and SEBS ([Andrews, Domke,
Murphy, Dimond, et al. 2026](#ref-andrews2026herringcapelin)). Bristol Bay sockeye salmon continued
to decline from peak 2021/2022 levels ([Cunningham et al. 2026](#ref-cunningham2026sockeye)). Strong
2020 and 2022 sablefish year classes contributed to a growing, aging population that could compete
for pelagic juvenile prey; direct evidence for that competition remained unavailable ([Siddon
2026](#ref-siddon2026ebs)).

### Predators

Adult pollock diets consisted primarily of copepods and euphausiids, with a low overall proportion
of cannibalism in 2026 ([Aydin 2026](#ref-aydin2026diets)). CNRG estimates showed that age-1 predation
mortality declined from 2025, while mortality due to cannibalism remained slightly above its
long-term mean. The biomass of pollock consumed by conspecifics was approximately average and lower
than in 2024 and 2025 ([Holsman et al. 2026](#ref-holsmanaydin2026cannibalism)). Adult Bristol Bay
sockeye salmon, which prey on juvenile pollock, decreased from 2025 ([Cunningham et al.
2026](#ref-cunningham2026sockeye)).

Northern fur seal pup weights at St. Paul Island exceeded the average by more than one standard
deviation, and maternal trip durations were the shortest in the time series. These indicators
suggested high foraging success near the island. Age-0 pollock and herring had the highest frequency
of occurrence in the September 2025 fur-seal diet samples; analysis of September 2026 samples was
ongoing in the draft ([McHuron et al. 2026](#ref-mchuron2026furseals)). The apex predator guild
increased from 2025, driven by a 17% increase in Pacific cod, and remained below its long-term mean
([Siddon 2026, 7--9](#ref-siddon2026ebs)). This guild level suggested low predation pressure on
juvenile pollock ([Siddon 2026](#ref-siddon2026ebs)).

## 11.2 Ecosystem considerations for later juveniles and adults {#sec-ecosystem-juveniles-adults}

### Distribution

Pollock biomass estimated by the standard bottom-trawl survey increased approximately 50% from 2025
to 2026, alongside a pronounced spatial pattern associated with the extensive cold pool. Adult
pollock occurred primarily outside bottom waters colder than 2°C, with concentrations along the
northwestern outer shelf ([Siddon 2026](#ref-siddon2026ebs)). The cold pool therefore delineated the
near-bottom habitat occupied by much of the adult population during the survey. This pattern is
relevant to interpreting the biomass increase because survey catches reflected both the number and
size of fish present and their availability to bottom-trawl gear. The higher survey estimate and the
concentration of adults along the cold-pool margin should be considered together when comparing
years. The spatial association supports a role for temperature in shaping survey availability, while
the contribution of redistribution to the biomass increase remains unresolved.

### Environmental Processes

Bottom temperatures in 2026 were comparable to the historical cool years 1986, 1992, 2006 and 2010
([Siddon 2026](#ref-siddon2026ebs)). The large cold pool provided further evidence of cool bottom
conditions ([Rohan and Barnett 2026](#ref-rohanbarnett2026coldpool)). Below-average SSTs
characterized the SEBS, particularly during spring ([Lemagie and Callahan
2026](#ref-lemagiecallahan2026sst)). Adult pollock condition was above its long-term mean ([Prohaska
and Rohan 2026](#ref-prohaskarohan2026condition)). These temperature and condition patterns described
concurrent conditions; their causal relationship remained an interpretation.

### Prey

Adult pollock diets continued to be dominated by copepods and euphausiids ([Aydin
2026](#ref-aydin2026diets)). Summer and late-summer euphausiid abundance increased from 2025 to 2026
([Levine et al. 2026](#ref-levine2026euphausiids); [Spear et al. 2026](#ref-spear2026euphausiids)),
and above-average SEBS copepod and euphausiid lipid content provided lipid-rich prey ([Pinger et al.
2026](#ref-pinger2026lipids)). Cannibalism formed a low proportion of adult pollock diets ([Aydin
2026](#ref-aydin2026diets)). CNRG estimates separately indicated slightly above-average mortality of
age-1 pollock from cannibalism, with approximately average biomass consumed by conspecifics
([Holsman et al. 2026](#ref-holsmanaydin2026cannibalism)).

Morphometric condition, measured as length--weight residuals, for large adult pollock (\>250 mm) in
the EBS survey increased from 2023 to 2026 to above the long-term mean. The NBS condition series
extended through 2025, when large-pollock condition remained positive and continued the increasing
trend observed since 2021 ([Prohaska and Rohan 2026](#ref-prohaskarohan2026condition)).

### Competitors

The increase in pelagic forager biomass from 2025 to 2026 was primarily driven by pollock ([Siddon
2026, 7--9](#ref-siddon2026ebs)), suggesting a potential increase in competition within the pollock
population. Above-average prey quantity, prey quality and pollock length--weight residuals indicated
adequate food resources. Increasing sablefish abundance represented potential competition for pelagic
prey, with direct evidence still pending ([Siddon 2026](#ref-siddon2026ebs)).

### Predators

The apex predator guild, driven by Pacific cod, increased from 2025 and remained below its long-term
mean ([Siddon 2026, 7--9](#ref-siddon2026ebs)). This pattern suggested low predation pressure on
pollock ([Siddon 2026](#ref-siddon2026ebs)). These associations provided context for the stock;
independent evidence was needed to establish the underlying mechanisms. The Plan Team requested
further examination of ecosystem contributions to retrospective behavior alongside the direct
data-influence tests.

# 12 Data gaps and research priorities

The 2026 assessment compared the separately fitted configurations and the Model 26.1.2
marginal-estimation sensitivity using their matching observations and conditional observation
diagnostics. Model 26.0 posterior uncertainty, predictive observation checks and nine retrospective
fits were complete. The Model 26.1.2 retrospective diagnostic used fixed full-model process SDs and a
conditional full 2026 reference. The two Model 26.0 simulation-retrospective experiments compared
conditional biomass and recruitment revisions with the observed-data results
([Section 6.3.1](#sec-model260-selftest)). Each experiment used ten simulated datasets to examine
biomass and recruitment revisions.

Additional age-1 BTS selectivity and BTS data-influence tests were outside the scope of this
assessment (PT-02 and PT-05). The comparisons described differences in retrospective patterns. The
weight-at-age comparison in [Section 4.1.3](#sec-fishery-weights) retained the distinction between
estimated schedules and uncertainty carried into population and projection outputs.

A high research priority is to refine the statistical treatment of length compositions and age
observations from the fishery, bottom-trawl survey (BTS), and acoustic-trawl survey (ATS), together
with paired Fourier-transform near-infrared spectroscopy (FT-NIR) and traditional morphological
ageing (TMA) observations. A more statistically rigorous framework should account for sampling
structure, ageing error, uncertainty in conversions between ageing methods, and dependence among
observations derived from the same samples. This work should guide composition weighting and the
integration of length and age information, with the resulting methods and uncertainty treatment
carried into future model specifications.

The treatment of early fishery data should also be refined relative to more recent observations.
Research should evaluate changes in sampling coverage, age and length information, and fishing
practices across periods, and use those differences to inform selectivity assumptions and
observation weights. Comparisons should assess how alternative treatments affect recruitment,
biomass trends, and retrospective behavior.

Further development of random-effects models should address temporal variation in selectivity and
other population or observation processes. Priorities include identifying which sources of
variability the data can resolve, evaluating correlation across ages and years, and estimating
process variation within a coherent framework. Simulation tests, retrospective analyses, and
predictive checks should evaluate model performance and the propagation of uncertainty into stock
status and catch projections.

Future assessments could explore alternative weighting methods for age composition data, such as the Dirichlet-multinomial distribution coupled with more
complete random-effects specifications. Such an approach may refine historical process-error penalty weights and would help assess whether estimating
this additional variation within the model improves the treatment of age-composition data and
changes the resulting stock estimates. In the process of adopting new data weighting practices, we encourage
checking that the resulting data weights remain sensible and robust.


The Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile (ESP) provides a basis for fuller implementation and use of
dynamic structural equation models (DSEM). This work should develop and test hypothesized links
among environmental conditions, prey, pollock condition, and recruitment, while accounting for
observation uncertainty, missing years, and time lags. Evaluation should establish the stability and
predictive value of these relationships and how ESP results can inform assessment interpretation,
recruitment scenarios, and future model specifications.

Additional research questions include AVO uncertainty, the 2018 recruitment profile, and stock
boundaries and connectivity.

[Source: AKFIN / NMFS Alaska Regional Office FMP catch export. Estimates sum retained and discarded catch across both pollock target categories and all reported gears in the BS subarea. Pollock, salmon, halibut, Non TAC Species, and records without a species group are excluded. Other combines remaining named source groups, including other flatfish and rockfish, Greenland turbot, Alaska plaice, squid, octopus, sculpins, and historical Other / Other Species groups; definitions follow the source export rather than a fixed modern FMP list. NA means no records for that category and year, rather than a measured zero. Source group names and the complete column map are available with the annual CSV. Values are summed before rounding; units are metric tons. The 2026 estimates are preliminary through the week ending October 24. Table 7:Pollock bycatch (t) in identified non-pollock directed Bering Sea fisheries, 1991-2026.

:::

[Source: AKFIN / NMFS Alaska Regional Office FMP catch export, BS subarea. Estimates include retained and discarded pollock catch and all reported gears. Pollock-directed trips, blank trip targets, and No retained catch targets are excluded. Other.flats combines flathead sole, arrowtooth flounder, other flatfish, Alaska plaice, Kamchatka flounder, and Greenland turbot targets. Other.spp combines the remaining identified targets: rockfish, sablefish, Atka mackerel, Other Species, and halibut. Rock.sole is the source Rock Sole - BSAI target; it is not restricted to a separately identified northern rock sole target. NA means no records for that target group and year. Total sums the included unrounded values; displayed columns may differ from Total by rounding. Units are metric tons. The 2026 estimates are preliminary through the week ending October 31. The complete target map and exclusion totals accompany the annual CSV. Table 8:Bycatch estimates of prohibited species in the BSAI midwater pollock fishery, 1991--2026.

:::

[Source: author-provided AKFIN / NMFS Alaska Regional Office export, received from AKR October 27, 2026 and loaded November 7, 2026 (earlier source dates remain in some historical records). Only trips classified as Pollock - midwater are included, with no additional gear or vessel-sector filter. Herring, halibut catch (Halib), and halibut mortality (Halib.M) are metric tons; other columns are estimated numbers of individuals. Values are summed before rounding. NA denotes unavailable estimates; zero denotes a reported zero. Sums use available values when individual records are missing; halibut mortality is unavailable for 1991--1993 and has some missing records in 1998--2003. The 2026 values are preliminary, through the week ending October 24. Other King Crab is outside the species columns of the example table. ::: {#tbl-nontarget-species-bycatch .report-table .unnumbered data-table="tables/014-tbl-nontarget-species-bycatch.csv"}

Table 9:Estimated catch (t) of selected nontarget-species groups in the BSAI directed pollock
fishery, 2003-2026.

:::

[Source: AKFIN / NMFS Alaska Regional Office nontarget catch-accounting export. BSAI records (BS and AI) are included; GOA and inside-water records are excluded. Both pollock target categories, all reported gears, and retained and discarded records are combined using Nontarget Estimate (mt), not the species-count field. Squid, sculpins, and seabirds are outside the selected groups of this table and are excluded. MiscFish is the source Misc fish group. Osmerid combines capelin, eulachon, other osmerids, family Osmeridae smelts, and surf smelt; Grenadier combines all named grenadier groups. Other contains the remaining selected fish and invertebrate groups; the complete mapping accompanies the annual CSV. NA means no records for a group-year; a displayed zero may be a positive estimate below 0.5 t. Values are summed before rounding to whole metric tons. The 2026 estimates are preliminary through the week ending October 24. The November 2024 summary approximately doubled the 2019-2022 Jellies, MiscFish, SeaStar, Osmerid, Grenadier, and Eelpouts columns relative to September. Sea pen, Anemone, Snails, and Other changed non-uniformly, with cross-column numerical matches indicating changed alignment or allocation. These are comparisons of historical headers. The current table uses explicit source species names and both catch dispositions, with no scaling adjustment. The upstream preparation step remains unconfirmed. [View the jellyfish source-history and filter audit](validation/jellyfish-audit.html). [Download annual estimates (CSV)](tables/nontarget-species-bycatch.csv) · [Column definitions (CSV)](tables/nontarget-species-column-map.csv).]{.small}

## Appendix B Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile of Eastern Bering Sea Walleye Pollock {#sec-esp-2026-appendix}

This draft Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile (ESP) for EBS pollock brings together substantial
work completed to date and provides a starting point for future ESP Team discussions. An AI agent
helped compile and coordinate material from disparate information sources and research activities.
Over the next year, the EBS pollock ESP Team will formalize its membership and begin meetings that
engage a broader group of scientific experts to develop the profile. Please contact Jim Ianelli and
Kalei Shotwell with questions or for further details about this document or the EBS pollock ESP.

![](assets/pollock-esp-hex-sticker.png){fig-alt="Pollock ESP hexagonal emblem with a fish silhouette and ecosystem, socioeconomic, and research imagery." .esp2026-logo}
