### Executive Summary {#esp2026-executive-summary}

The Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile (ESP) connected stock-specific environmental, biological,
fishery, and community information with assessment interpretation and management questions. Its
sequence of focus, synthesis, analysis, and communication provided a structured way to evaluate
proposed indicators ([Shotwell et al. 2023](#ref-esp2026-shotwell2023esp)). This draft focuses
initially on recruitment to age 1, then identified processes affecting juvenile survival to age 3,
adult growth and condition, survey interpretation, and fishery performance.

The ESP distinguished two DSEM applications. The archived Rceattle pilot evaluated birth-year SST
and age-1-year cold-pool proxies ([Ianelli et al. 2026](#ref-esp2026-ianelli2026developments)). A
separate age-1 DSEM working paper analyzes 18 ecosystem series alongside an age-1 response estimated
by the assessment. Regional age-0 energy density provided an additional measured-condition series
([Page and Maselko 2026](#ref-esp2026-page2026energy)).

#### Acceptable Biological Catch Considerations {#esp2026-acceptable-biological-catch-considerations}

##### Candidate Predictive Indicators {#esp2026-candidate-predictive-indicators}

Fall age-0 total energy, prey quality and abundance, and juvenile--predator overlap were priorities
for testing. Field studies connect fall total energy with age-1 recruits per spawner, and laboratory
experiments identify body size and energy reserves as determinants of survival during food
deprivation ([Heintz et al. 2013](#ref-esp2026-heintz2013); [Sogard and Olla
2000](#ref-esp2026-sogard2000)). Studies of pollock recruitment and spatial predation identify
juvenile overlap with adult pollock and arrowtooth flounder as another important pathway ([Mueter et
al. 2006](#ref-esp2026-mueter2006); [Spencer et al. 2016](#ref-esp2026-spencer2016)).

The regional energy-density series contain 21 southeastern Bering Sea (SEBS) and 15 northern Bering
Sea (NBS) annual means within 2002--2025, measured in kJ/g dry mass. The latest values, for 2025,
were 19.23 and 20.84 kJ/g dry mass for SEBS and NBS, respectively. Both were lower than their 2024
observations; a 2026 energy-density observation was absent. Sampling metadata, observation
uncertainty, and forecast evaluation remain prerequisites for a predictive role ([Page and Maselko
2026](#ref-esp2026-page2026energy)).

##### Contextual Indicators {#esp2026-contextual-indicators}

Sea ice, seasonal temperature, cold-pool extent, plankton and euphausiids, age-0 abundance and
condition, adult condition, weight-at-age, and predator overlap form the initial contextual set. The
relevant biological question was whether each cohort encounters adequate prey, accumulates energy
before winter, and survives subsequent predation. The poor 2007 cohort illustrates why a favorable
temperature category alone can give an incomplete account: low summer production and poor age-0
condition occurred during a cold year ([Gann et al. 2016](#ref-esp2026-gann2016)).

The 2026 physical and prey indicators show a mixed pattern relative to their own observed-period
means. Sea ice and cold-pool extent were above those means; SST and bottom temperature were below. The
open-water bloom indicator was lower, while chlorophyll a was higher. Spring small and large copepods
and summer small copepods were below their respective means; summer large copepods were slightly
above. [](#esp2026-recorded-annual-indicators)

##### Fishery Informed Indicators {#esp2026-fishery-informed-indicators}

Candidate indicators include age and size composition of catch, fishery weight-at-age, season and
area of harvest, standardized fishery catch rates, catch and quota utilization, and salmon bycatch
measures. Their interpretation must account for fishing choices, allocation and avoidance behavior,
processing demand, and reporting coverage. These indicators may reveal operational changes or
sampling differences that help interpret assessment inputs. Their proposed inclusion in this ESP
required a defined management question.

The draft supported evaluation of ecosystem and fishery concerns in the SAFE risk table. Any
resulting change in risk classification or ABC must be documented by the assessment authors using
the completed annual synthesis and assessment results. ABC and OFL remain unchanged by this
contribution.

#### Total Allowable Catch Considerations {#esp2026-total-allowable-catch-considerations}

Verified economic context covers BSAI catch, participation, ex-vessel and first-wholesale statistics
through 2024, and U.S.-national trade through 2025 ([Catch and Market
Context](#esp2026-economic-observations)). These scopes differ from the BS assessment stock and from
each other. A speculative 2026 interpretation was that firmer product unit values could support
gross returns, while operating costs and product mix could offset those gains unevenly among
vessels, processors and communities. 2026 margins and community outcomes remain uncertain. This
interpretation was qualitative.

### Responses to SSC and Plan Team Comments on ESPs in General {#esp2026-responses-to-ssc-and-plan-team-comments-on-esps-in-general}

A summary of potential SSC/PT comments on ESPs in general included: distinguish predictive from
contextual indicators, evaluate competing mechanistic explanations, document DSEM diagnostics, and
coordinate economic and community information with existing Council products. This pollock
contribution addresses those questions by defining indicator roles, documenting the fitted pilot and
its diagnostic limitation, and proposing an explicit socioeconomic inventory.

### Responses to SSC and Plan Team Comments Specific to EBS Pollock {#esp2026-responses-to-ssc-and-plan-team-comments-specific-to-ebs-pollock}

December 2024 SSC, EBS Ecosystem Status Report (page 3): the SSC recommended pollock-focused
DSEM work to reconcile contrasting larval, juvenile-condition, and adult signals, and to investigate
changed recruitment relationships ([North Pacific Fishery Management Council Scientific and
Statistical Committee 2024](#ref-esp2026-npfmc2024ssc)).

Contribution to that work: The starter age-1 DSEM analysis appears in the 2026 EBS Ecosystem
Status Report (Siddon 2026).[](#ref-esp2026-siddon2026coordination)

The assessment website records continuing work on contrasting early-life observations, cannibalism
and biomass consumed, multispecies mortality, weight-at-age and condition, and stock distribution
across U.S. and Russian waters ([EBS Pollock Assessment Team 2026](#ref-esp2026-ianelli2026ssc)).
Its retained earlier responses carry an explicit requirement for verification before use as final
results. This draft translates those topics into proposed ESP tasks.

Pollock review topics and proposed ESP contributions were summarized in [Table B1](#esp2026-tbl-review).

### Introduction {#esp2026-introduction}

Pollock recruitment reflected survival through several life stages with different food requirements,
habitats, and predator exposure. Large differences in egg or larval abundance can be modified by
later feeding, growth, transport, and mortality. The first-year review by Duffy-Anderson et
al. provided the organizing synthesis for these processes ([Duffy-Anderson et al.
2016](#ref-esp2026-duffyanderson2016)). The local recruitment review extended that structure through
ages 1 and 2 to survival at age 3. In this appendix, age-1 recruitment was the focal response
used by the DSEM pilot; survival to age 3 was a separate later-stage outcome that retained the
identity of the same birth cohort.

#### Justification {#esp2026-justification}

The ESP creates an evidence trail from a biological or socioeconomic question to an indicator and
its proposed use. For EBS pollock, the immediate question was whether early-life information can
improve interpretation of uncertain recruitment and future biomass. Additional questions concern
adult productivity, changing spatial availability to surveys, fishery operations, and community
exposure. The September 2026 document provided the starting framework for developing this appendix
([Ianelli et al. 2026](#ref-esp2026-ianelli2026developments)).

#### Data {#esp2026-data}

##### Age-0 Energy Density {#esp2026-contributor--age-0-energy-density}

Annual mean energy density of age-0 walleye pollock was available for the northern and southeastern
Bering Sea during 2002--2025, in kJ/g dry mass ([Page and Maselko
2026](#ref-esp2026-page2026energy)). Johanna Page (Vollenweider) provided the data, with Jacek
Maselko as a co-contact. The southeastern series contained 21 annual means and the northern series
contained 15. Both regions lack observations for 2003, 2013 and 2020; the northern series also lacks
2008--2012 and 2014.

The source inventory and remaining data-assembly needs were summarized in [Table B2](#esp2026-tbl-data).

### Indicator Synthesis {#esp2026-indicator-synthesis}

#### Ecosystem Processes {#esp2026-ecosystem-processes}

##### Spawning Supply and Transport {#esp2026-spawning-supply-and-transport}

Spawning biomass and spawning location influence egg and early-larval supply. Smart et al. found
associations between spawning biomass and early stages, with weaker correspondence after early
larval development ([Smart et al. 2012](#ref-esp2026-smart2012)). Transport and the spatial
arrangement of spawning also matter. The biophysical model of Petrik et al. reproduced warm--cold
distribution differences most successfully through changes in spawning areas ([Petrik et al.
2015](#ref-esp2026-petrik2015)). These results supported separate hypotheses for cohort supply,
transport, and access to nursery habitat.

##### Feeding and Fall Age-0 Condition {#esp2026-feeding-and-fall-age-0-condition}

Prey availability included amount, nutritional quality, and spatial match with fish. Larval copepod
concentrations and frontal habitat illustrate why a broad regional biomass index can differ from
prey encountered by an individual fish ([Smart et al. 2012](#ref-esp2026-smart2012); [Brodeur et al.
2000](#ref-esp2026-brodeur2000)). Diet studies show that prey use varied with fish size and that
pollock and Pacific cod can partition prey ([Buckley et al. 2016](#ref-esp2026-buckley2016);
[Strasburger et al. 2014](#ref-esp2026-strasburger2014)).

Siddon et al. describe a seasonal shift from larval growth and development toward lipid storage
after transformation to the juvenile stage ([Siddon et al. 2013](#ref-esp2026-siddon2013)). Heintz
et al. found higher diet lipid content and age-0 energy density during cold conditions in their
study; fall total energy was positively associated with age-1 recruits per spawner ([Heintz et al.
2013](#ref-esp2026-heintz2013)). Moss et al. also documented differences in age-0 energetic
condition and food habits across thermal conditions ([Moss et al. 2009](#ref-esp2026-moss2009)).
These findings motivate indicators of energy density, body mass, and total energy with explicit
measurement definitions. The annual series measures energy density in kJ/g dry mass.

Eisner et al. evaluated large copepods as leading indicators of age-3 pollock abundance for the
2002--2015 year classes, excluding 2013 ([Eisner et al. 2020](#ref-esp2026-eisner2020copepods)).
Their comparison reinforces the value of prey information while identifying a specific cohort range
and recruitment age.

##### Overwinter Survival {#esp2026-overwinter-survival}

Fall condition provided the starting reserves for the first winter. Sogard and Olla's
food-deprivation experiments show that greater size, higher initial condition, and colder water can
extend survival ([Sogard and Olla 2000](#ref-esp2026-sogard2000)). Field survival also involves
winter feeding, movement, and predators. Laboratory results therefore support a mechanism and its
direction, while annual field data were needed to quantify its effect on recruitment.

Sea ice, bloom timing, summer mixing, and temperature influence prey production and energy demand.
Sigler et al. connect annual production of copepods, euphausiids, and juvenile pollock with seasonal
environmental conditions ([Sigler et al. 2016](#ref-esp2026-sigler2016)). Gann et al.'s analysis of
2007 identifies a plausible production limitation during a cold year ([Gann et al.
2016](#ref-esp2026-gann2016)). The ESP should evaluate these intermediate processes before
interpreting a simple warm--cold contrast as a cohort forecast.

##### Predation and Later Juvenile Survival {#esp2026-predation-and-later-juvenile-survival}

Adult pollock can increase juvenile mortality through cannibalism, while arrowtooth flounder and
other predators create additional exposure. Mueter et al. identify both food-related and
predation-related controls on pollock recruitment, including juvenile--adult overlap ([Mueter et al.
2006](#ref-esp2026-mueter2006)). Spencer et al. model spatial predation by arrowtooth flounder and
show how cold-pool extent can alter predator access to juvenile habitat ([Spencer et al.
2016](#ref-esp2026-spencer2016)).

The timing of predation matters for the response. A summer overlap or cold-pool observation in year
$t+1$ occurs after the beginning of the cohort's age-1 year. Its use to explain an age-1 entry state
required explicit justification or a revised response definition. Such observations may be more
directly aligned with survival during age 1 and later ages.

::: {#esp2026-adult-productivity-and-observation-processes .section}
Life stages, processes and priority observations are summarized in [Table B3](#esp2026-tbl-life-history).
:::

##### Workshop Conceptual Models for Recruitment and Growth {#esp2026-workshop-conceptual-models-for-recruitment-and-growth}

The January 2025 pollock biology and ecology workshop developed preliminary conceptual models for
Bering Sea recruitment and growth ([Monnahan et al. 2026](#ref-esp2026-monnahan2026workshop)).
[Figure B1](#esp2026-fig-workshop-recruitment) organizes reproductive output, seasonal juvenile
stages, prey quality, energetic condition, predation, and cold-pool extent.
[Figure B2](#esp2026-fig-workshop-growth) connected population weight-at-age with somatic growth,
size-selective mortality, prey, competitors, fishing, and physical conditions. Together they supported
an ESP that examined recruitment and growth.

Recruitment pathways: spawning biomass and fecundity inform reproductive output. Seasonal
surveys track the cohort from spring age 0 through age 2. Diet, krill, copepods, and prey lipid
measurements inform forage quality and juvenile energetic condition; predation indices and cold-pool
extent inform later survival. The diagram highlights both candidate observations and intermediate
biological states.

Growth pathways: the model separated growth of surviving fish from changes in population
weight-at-age associated with size-selective mortality. Prey availability, density, genetic
diversity, and spatial history enter the growth network alongside physical conditions and
zooplankton. This distinction supported age- and season-specific weight and condition indicators with
explicit survey or fishery sampling definitions.

The cohort sequence in [Figure B3](#esp2026-fig-pathways) summarized the recruitment mechanisms
developed in this draft and extended the survival question to age 3. The workshop diagrams provide a
broader set of hypotheses for future indicator development.

#### Socioeconomic Processes {#esp2026-socioeconomic-processes}

Biological supply, access to fishing grounds, operating costs, product demand, and processing
capacity can jointly affect realized harvest and its value. Those processes may alter where and when
vessels fish, the size and age of fish landed, and the distribution of benefits. This component
should therefore connect each indicator to a concrete question, such as whether lower quota
utilization reflects reduced fish availability, market conditions, processing limits, or avoidance
behavior.

The Economic SAFE provided source categories for catch, discards, prohibited species catch,
production and value, participation, and effort ([Alaska Fisheries Science Center
2026b](#ref-esp2026-noaa2026economic)). This draft proposes species- and sector-specific summaries
where the source reports that detail. Community analysis required clear distinctions among landing
ports, vessel ownership, workforce residence, processor location, and CDQ beneficiaries. Each
described a different form of participation or exposure.

#### Proposed Indicators {#esp2026-proposed-indicators}

The mechanism table ([Table B4](#esp2026-tbl-mechanisms)) links a driver, a measurable process, and
the intended response. Expected directions were hypotheses for the stated pathway. Several upstream
physical effects depend on season, prey response, and spatial coverage, so their net sign can change
across conditions.

### Indicator Assessment {#esp2026-indicator-assessment}

#### Indicator Selection {#esp2026-indicator-selection}

Selection starts with a mechanistic explanation, the population or socioeconomic response, and the
date when the information becomes available. Candidates then require reliable annual production,
adequate spatial and temporal coverage, quantified uncertainty, and additional information beyond
the other indicators.

##### Ecosystem Indicators {#esp2026-ecosystem-indicators}

The initial set should remain small enough for scientific review: seasonal physical forcing; a
documented prey index; fall age-0 size and energetic condition; juvenile--predator overlap or a
reviewed mortality product; and adult growth and condition. Larval supply and transport add value
when the data cover enough years and the indicators are biologically comparable. Indicator families should be assessed
together so correlated temperature, ice, and prey signals receive an interpretation that accounts
for shared processes.

The available age-0 energy-density series describe regional energetic condition ([Figure
B4](#esp2026-fig-energy-density)). The histories of the ecosystem inputs and age-1 response provide
context for the DSEM analysis ([Figure B5](#esp2026-fig-working-indicators)).

##### Socioeconomic Indicators {#esp2026-socioeconomic-indicators}

Proposed socioeconomic indicator families, measures and management questions were summarized in
[Table B5](#esp2026-tbl-socioeconomic).

##### Catch and Market Context {#esp2026-economic-observations}

The broader Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands (BSAI) pollock fishery reported 1.3163 million tons of
total catch in 2024 ([Table B6](#esp2026-tbl-catch-exvessel-economics)). Trawl catcher vessels
retained 678.40 thousand tons, with an ex-vessel value of \$213.43 million. These economic
statistics cover the BSAI; their area and accounting definitions differ from the BS stock-assessment
catch series. Published pollock-target vessel counts were 103 across harvesting sectors and 76
catcher vessels. The counts describe participation in the target fishery and include their
source-specific gear definitions.

Published first-wholesale pollock production was 487.89 thousand tons of product weight and \$1.4743
billion in 2024 ([Table B7](#esp2026-tbl-first-wholesale-economics)). The Economic SAFE excluded
confidential components from some aggregates; the combined fillet quantities and derived values for
2021--2022 remain unavailable here. Product mix and market conditions both affect the observed unit
values ([Abelman et al. 2026](#ref-esp2026-abelman2026economic)).

Global Alaska pollock capture production was 3.573 million tons in 2024 ([Table
B8](#esp2026-tbl-trade-global), panel A). The United States and Russian Federation accounted for
39.9% and 54.0%, respectively, and BSAI catch represented about 36.8% of the global total. U.S.
Alaska-pollock domestic exports totaled 333 thousand tons of products valued at \$1.00 billion in
2025, compared with 332 thousand tons and \$0.946 billion in 2024 (panel B). These national trade
statistics extend through 2025; global catch statistics extend through 2024. Their product weights,
nominal export values and legacy import/destination baskets were defined in the table notes ([FAO
2026](#ref-esp2026-fao2026capture); [NOAA Fisheries 2026](#ref-esp2026-noaa2026trade)).

Among the three destination groups shown, selected European countries accounted for the largest
export shares throughout 2020--2025 ([Figure B6](#esp2026-fig-export-destinations)). Meat's share of
export volume rose from 45.8% in 2020 to 53.3% in 2025, while its value share rose from 44.0% to
53.0% ([Figure B7](#esp2026-fig-export-product-mix)). The Russian Federation accounted for more than
half of global catch in each year from 2020 to 2024 ([Figure B8](#esp2026-fig-global-catch-origin)).
First-wholesale surimi volume declined from 185.5 to 165.1 thousand tons between 2023 and 2024,
while fillet volume rose from 142.9 to 158.6 thousand tons ([Figure
B9](#esp2026-fig-first-wholesale-products)).

#### Annual Indicator Status {#esp2026-annual-indicator-status}

##### Age-0 Energy Density Through 2025 {#esp2026-age-0-energy-density-through-2025}

The latest five available observation years were 2021--2025
([Table B9](#esp2026-tbl-energy-density)). In 2025, the SEBS annual mean was 19.23 kJ/g dry mass,
0.64 lower than in 2024. The NBS annual mean was 20.84, 0.09 lower than in 2024 ([Page and Maselko
2026](#ref-esp2026-page2026energy)). These were descriptive differences between annual means.

##### Annual Indicator Series {#esp2026-recorded-annual-indicators}

The age-1 DSEM input spans 1964--2026 and contained 18 ecosystem series plus the assessment-derived
age-1 response ([Figure B5](#esp2026-fig-working-indicators)). Seventeen ecosystem series had 2026
values; the energy-density series ended in 2025, and age-1 observations end in 2024.

Standardized departures below equal each value minus that series' mean, divided by its sample
standard deviation. Each baseline used all available finite observations, including the latest year,
and retained the series' gaps. These baselines were descriptive historical variability, rather than a
common fixed climatology, sampling-error intervals or approved biological thresholds.

In 2026, sea ice was +0.89 SD relative to its 1985--2026 baseline of 42 observations. Cold-pool
extent was +1.12 SD, SST −0.39 SD and bottom temperature −0.79 SD relative to their separate
1982--2026 baselines of 44 available observations each. Sea ice and cold pool both exceed their 2025
values. SST also increased from 2025 despite remaining below its observed-period mean, whereas
bottom temperature fell.

The open-water bloom indicator was −1.54 SD and chlorophyll a was +0.77 SD relative to their separate
1998--2026 baselines of 29 observations each. Both declined from their 2025 values. Spring small and
large copepods were −0.45 and −0.66 SD using their separate 2000--2026 baselines of 25 observations;
summer small and large copepods were −0.92 and +0.21 SD using their separate 2003--2026 baselines of
22 observations. The mixed physical and prey pattern supported contextual discussion rather than an
overall favorable or adverse recruitment classification.

#### Indicator Analysis {#esp2026-indicator-analysis}

The September 2026 assessment development document presents a pilot DSEM analysis of SST and
cold-pool pathways (Ianelli et al. 2026). Tables B10--B11 reproduce its fit comparisons and direct
proxy coefficients as an example of analyses that could be provided in the ESP.

##### Decision Support {#esp2026-decision-support}

A contextual indicator may inform the SAFE risk-table discussion when it identified a documented
condition relevant to recruitment, productivity, survey interpretation, or fishery operations. Its
influence on a risk category required an explanation of the evidence and uncertainty. A predictive
indicator needs forecast evaluation and numerical checks. Incorporation into an assessment
likelihood, projections, or a harvest rule required a separate, reviewed implementation and
evaluation of effects on biomass, uncertainty, ABC, and OFL.

##### Socioeconomic Monitoring {#esp2026-socioeconomic-monitoring}

Socioeconomic monitoring can build on the main assessment's discussion of fishery conditions,
including fishing locations, catch rates, effort, size composition, and bycatch avoidance, alongside
economic performance, participation, and community exposure. The catch-decision indicators and
probabilities in Tables 55 and 56 provide a framework for comparing alternative catches in terms of
fishing mortality, future spawning biomass, age composition, and relative fishing pressure. The
fishing-mortality-based effort proxy describes relative pressure; observed vessel effort,
catchability, operating costs, and revenues would provide the economic context for interpreting it.
Future ESP drafts will pursue incorporating these fishery-condition observations and decision-table
comparisons to connect projected stock outcomes with operational and socioeconomic consequences.

### Data Gaps and Future Research Priorities {#esp2026-data-gaps-and-future-research-priorities}

#### Ecosystem Priorities {#esp2026-ecosystem-priorities}

One of our priorities was cohort-aligned predator overlap or mortality, with timing that matched the
survival interval. Joint juvenile and predator distributions, diet and consumption estimates, and
direct fall--spring cohort comparisons would strengthen interpretation.

Transport and nursery delivery, prey timing and lipid content, winter exposure, and annual
observation-error estimates remain additional priorities. Climate relationships should be assessed
for stability across recent warm conditions and historical regimes. Long-term climate projections in
Mueter et al. and Spencer et al. describe conditional scenarios ([Mueter et al.
2011](#ref-esp2026-mueter2011); [Spencer et al. 2016](#ref-esp2026-spencer2016)); their projected
effects provided research context rather than annual 2026 indicator values.

#### Socioeconomic Priorities {#esp2026-socioeconomic-priorities}

Confirm a compact pollock-specific indicator set with economic and social science contributors.
Resolve sector and community definitions, annual update capacity, disclosure rules, cost
comparability, and a common price base. Evaluate whether incomplete quota utilization or altered
fishing patterns had identifiable operational, market, processing, or biological causes. Document
the availability date for each product so the ESP distinguished information usable during the
specification process from information released later.

#### Completion Priorities for the 2026 Appendix {#esp2026-completion-priorities-for-the-2026-appendix}

Confirm the primary sources, units, seasonal and spatial definitions and observation uncertainty for
the working annual series. Review the age-1 DAG and the proposed energy and predator pathways with
the ESP and ecosystem teams. Preserve separate timing and scaling for the archived Rceattle pilot
and standalone DSEM, and retain the AR1 forecast benchmark when evaluating any expanded model.
Reconcile the historical pilot archive and its outstanding numerical checks before using the
indicators to support an annual status or risk classification.

::: {#esp2026-template-completion .section}
:::

### Conclusion {#esp2026-conclusion}

The literature supported following cohorts through spawning and delivery, prey and fall age-0 energy,
first-winter survival, and later predator exposure. The ESP also considers adult productivity,
survey availability and socioeconomic conditions. The regional energy-density series supplied a
measured-condition indicator through 2025.

Economic observations extend through 2024 for the BSAI fishery and 2025 for national trade; the 2026
interpretation was qualitative.

## Appendix C Research and Other Noncommercial Pollock Removals {#sec-other-removals}

### Reported noncommercial catch

Reported noncommercial pollock catches in the Bering Sea were summarized by collection in [Table
C1](#app-table-b1) and by year in [Table C2](#app-table-b2). The AKR dataset covers 1982--2025
across the Gulf of Alaska, Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands; Bering Sea records begin in 1991, with
broader multisurvey coverage from 2010. These were reported collection-year amounts, rather than
verified complete EBS-stock totals. Missing years and collection cells indicate absent observations.
The data ended in 2025.

The summaries used the reported Bering Sea FMP area, retaining stations from collections whose names
mention other regions. Explicitly Bogoslof-named surveys were shown separately; other collections in
reporting area 518 remain among the other reported Bering Sea catches. In 2024, the total was
216.280081 t, including 4.393640 t from the named Bogoslof survey and 211.886441 t from other
reported Bering Sea collections. The corresponding 2025 reported total was 140.994428 t.

Experimental fishing permit (EFP) records account for 1,198.506090 t in 2011 and 771.516610 t in
2021. Their inclusion explains the large totals in those years. The sole 2020 record was a Bogoslof
collection; other EBS research removals remain unverified for that year. Historical EFP inclusion in
official catch accounting required reconciliation. AKR metadata state that no 2025 EFP catches
occurred outside CAS.

Weights were converted from kilograms to tons using the units corroborated by [AKR dataset
correspondence](https://mail.google.com/mail/u/?authuser=jim.ianelli%40noaa.gov#all/1a13617188c1ece3),
dated 9 October and forwarded on 13 October 2026. Annual completeness of the AKR dataset received on
27 October remained unverified. The 2020--2023 totals agree, after rounding, with the accepted 2024
SAFE's research-catch table ([Ianelli et al. 2024](#ref-ianelli2024safe)). Noncommercial removals
were reported separately from assessment catch. The full annual summaries and source record retain
the collection details and reporting qualifications.

### Exempted fishing and other removal categories

The 2025 EFP 2025-01 permit and 2026 renewal allow up to 3,000 t of total groundfish, rather
than pollock alone, to be exempt from TAC during each permit's effective period; additional
groundfish catch counts against TAC. This authorization ceiling was separate from observed removals.
Actual pollock catch under these permitted and its accounting treatment require permit-specific
records.

EFP 2024-02 provided a footrope/gear exemption and otherwise retained applicable regulations. It
supplied no basis for assuming a TAC exemption. The noncommercial dataset included BS-labelled
subsistence records in 1991 and 1994; complete recent stock-specific subsistence, recreational and
other-FMP removals remain unverified.

## Appendix F Model Equations {#sec-model-equations}

Scope. This appendix carried forward the structure and model components of the 2024 *Appendix
EBS Pollock Model Description* (SAFE pp. 172--182). The equations describe the Model 23.0 ADMB
comparison. The proposed Model 26.0 configuration and its weight schedules were described in
[Section 5](#sec-approach) and [Section 4.1.3](#sec-fishery-weights). The historical Tier 1 material
documents an available calculation; the December 2024 SSC adopted Tier 3a.

### Dynamics

The statistical age-structured model combined the catch equation with annual survival and an
accumulating terminal age group ([Fournier and Archibald 1982](#ref-Fournier1982); [Hilborn and
Walters 1992](#ref-hilborn1992); [Schnute and Richards 1995](#ref-schnute1995); [McAllister and
Ianelli 1997](#ref-mcallister1997)). Let $t$ index years, $a=1,\ldots,A$ index ages, and $A=15$
denote ages 15 and older. $N_{t,a}$ was abundance at the start of the year, $F_{t,a}$ and $M_{t,a}$
were annual instantaneous mortality rates, and $Z_{t,a}$ was their sum. Catch at age and catch biomass
were

[]{#eq-admb-catch}

$$
\begin{aligned}
Z_{t,a}&=F_{t,a}+M_{t,a},\\
C_{t,a}&=N_{t,a}\frac{F_{t,a}}{Z_{t,a}}(1-e^{-Z_{t,a}}),\\
Y_t&=\sum_{a=1}^{A}C_{t,a}w^{f}_{t,a},\qquad
p^f_{t,a}=\frac{C_{t,a}}{\sum_b C_{t,b}}.
\end{aligned}
 \qquad(2)
$$

Here $w^f_{t,a}$ is fishery weight-at-age. Abundance in millions of fish multiplied by kg per fish
gives biomass in kt. The population advances as

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_{t+1,1}&=R_{t+1},\\
N_{t+1,a+1}&=N_{t,a}e^{-Z_{t,a}}, &&1\leq a<A,\\
N_{t+1,A}&=N_{t,A-1}e^{-Z_{t,A-1}}+N_{t,A}e^{-Z_{t,A}}.
\end{aligned}
 \qquad(3)
$$

The middle line applied to entry from each younger age; the final line added surviving members of the
plus group. This corrects the age subscript in 2024 Eq. 14.2, which printed $a-1$ on the right side
while advancing $a$ to $a+1$ on the left.

Fishing mortality separated annual intensity from selectivity at age:

$$
F_{t,a}=s^f_{t,a}\mu_F e^{\epsilon_t}.
 \qquad(4)
$$

The assessment estimates selectivity coefficients with penalties on changes over time and on
curvature across ages ([Butterworth et al. 2003](#ref-butterworth2003ajms)). In a general penalty
notation, $\Delta_t\log s_{t,a}$ controls annual changes and $\Delta_a^2\log s_{t,a}$ controls
smoothness across ages. Their weights and allowed change years come from the run controls.

The bottom-trawl survey (BTS) used logistic selectivity above age one and a separate age-one term.
The implemented form was

$$
\begin{aligned}
s^{b}_{t,a}&=\{1+\exp[-k_t(a-a_{50,t})]\}^{-1}, &&a>1,\\
\log s^{b}_{t,1}&=b_1\exp(d_t),\\
k_t&=\bar k\exp(u_t),\qquad a_{50,t}=\bar a_{50}\exp(v_t).
\end{aligned}
 \qquad(5)
$$

This followed `compute_selectivity()` and the age-one assignment in `Get_Selectivity()`. It replaces
the ambiguous slope/intercept and age-one expressions printed in 2024. The 2024 description reported
a process variance of 0.04 for an earlier random-walk formulation. The retained controls instead
select the penalty on changes in log-selectivity at the specified ages, plus the separate age-one
deviation penalty. Its coefficient was 8 for the squared first differences of $d_t$. The actual
controls and source identify which parameter or log-selectivity penalty was applied.

Acoustic-trawl survey (ATS) selectivity was flexible across ages; the optional separate age-one index
leaves ages 2--15+ in its composition likelihood. Constant survey catchability and time-varying
selectivity represent separate model components.

### Recruitment

Recruitment was abundance at age one. Female spawning biomass accounted for survival from the start of
the year to spawning:

$$
B_t=\sum_{a=1}^{A}N_{t,a}\exp(-\tau Z_{t,a})\phi_a w^s_{t,a},
\qquad \tau=0.25.
 \qquad(6)
$$

Here $w^s_{t,a}$ is spawning weight and $\phi_a$ includes both maturity and the female fraction. The
assessment reads a maturity schedule and applies the female fraction internally; the one-sex SPM
handoff reads maturity and halves total abundance. Applying the female fraction once preserves the
same biomass definition. The spawning time is April 1 (month 4).

Annual recruitment deviations accompany a stock--recruit function,
$R_t=f(B_{t-1})\exp(\varepsilon_t)$, with log-scale deviation penalties and the implementation's
bias adjustment. The Ricker option selected by `SrType=1` was

$$
f(B)=\frac{B}{\psi_0}\exp\!\left[\alpha_R\left(1-\frac{B}{B_0}\right)\right],
\qquad B_0=R_0\psi_0,\qquad
\alpha_R=\log\!\left(\frac{4h_{\mathrm{ADMB}}}{1-h_{\mathrm{ADMB}}}\right).
 \qquad(7)
$$

$\psi_0$ was unfished spawning biomass per recruit. The final expression was the source code's transformation of its parameter named steepness; it was retained as $h_{\mathrm{ADMB}}$ to identify that convention. The 2024 printed Ricker equation misplaced $R_0$ in the biomass ratio. The expression here followed `SRecruit()` and `Get_Bzero()` in the preserved template.

The alternative Beverton--Holt relationship ([Francis 1992](#ref-francis1992use)) was

$$
f_{\mathrm{BH}}(B)=\frac{B}{\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}}+\beta_{\mathrm{BH}}B},\qquad
\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}}=\psi_0\frac{1-h}{4h},\qquad
\beta_{\mathrm{BH}}=\frac{5h-1}{4hR_0}.
 \qquad(8)
$$

For this alternative, $h$ was the fraction of unfished recruitment at 20% of unfished spawning
biomass. The 2024 controls fix $\sigma_R=1$ and specify a symmetric beta prior with shape parameters
14.93209877 for the selected stock--recruit parameter. The earlier Beverton--Holt example in the
2024 appendix used a different prior; it remained an alternative rather than the selected 2024
setting.

### Diagnostics

The historical replay diagnostic retained fitted recruitment anomalies while adjusting recruitment
for the change in spawning biomass under a hypothetical history with fishing set to zero:

$$
R'_t=\widehat R_t\frac{f(B'_{t-1})}{f(B_{t-1})}.
 \qquad(9)
$$

Retrospective analyses repeat estimation after removing recent years and compare estimates for
common years ([Parma 1993](#ref-parma1993); [Ianelli and Fournier 1998](#ref-ianelli1998)). Their
fit controls and terminal years accompany each saved run.

The effective number of ages contributing to spawning biomass was the exponential of Shannon entropy
([Jost 2006](#ref-jost2006)):

$$
D_t=\exp\!\left(-\sum_a p^{B}_{t,a}\log p^{B}_{t,a}\right),\qquad
p^{B}_{t,a}=\frac{N_{t,a}e^{-\tau Z_{t,a}}\phi_a w^s_{t,a}}{B_t}.
 \qquad(10)
$$

The mean-age diagnostic used observed and predicted composition means and the predicted variance at
age ([Francis 2011](#ref-francis2011weighting)):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar a_t&=\sum_a a p_{t,a},\qquad
\widehat{\bar a}_t=\sum_a a\widehat p_{t,a},\\
V_t&=\sum_a(a-\widehat{\bar a}_t)^2\widehat p_{t,a},\\
z_t&=\frac{\bar a_t-\widehat{\bar a}_t}{\sqrt{V_t/n_t}},\qquad
\nu=\{\operatorname{Var}_t(z_t)\}^{-1}.
\end{aligned}
 \qquad(11)
$$

The implied adjusted sample size was $\nu n_t$. This diagnostic supported evaluation of weighting;
changing assessment inputs required a decision. The expression for $V_t$ replaces the malformed
$\kappa_t$ formula in the printed 2024 appendix.

### Parameter estimation

The objective added negative log likelihoods, prior densities and selectivity penalties. Phase-based
estimation introduces parameters in stages. For age compositions, the multinomial contribution, up
to a data-only constant, was

$$
\ell_{\mathrm{age}}=-\sum_t n_t\sum_a p_{t,a}\log(\widehat p_{t,a}+c),
\qquad \widehat{\boldsymbol p}^{\,\mathrm{read}}_t
=\widehat{\boldsymbol p}^{\,\mathrm{true}}_t E.
 \qquad(12)
$$

$c$ was the small numerical constant in the implementation. When enabled, $E_{a,b}$ was the probability that true age $a$ was read as age $b$. The selected historical controls had `use_age_err=0`. The original appendix also described a robust composition option ([Fournier et al. 1990](#ref-fournier1990multifan)), with variance inflation and a small outlier component. In the retained 2024 controls its activation phase was 1350; the six-phase completed comparison used the multinomial form. This distinction prevents the general software description from implying that the robust option was active.

For survey $s$ at within-year time $\tau_s$, expected abundance and biomass at age were

$$
\widehat N^s_{t,a}=q_s s^s_{t,a}N_{t,a}e^{-\tau_s Z_{t,a}},\qquad
\widehat I^s_t=\sum_a\widehat N^s_{t,a}w^s_{t,a}.
 \qquad(13)
$$

An abundance index omitted the weight multiplier. The original description used midyear survey timing;
actual run inputs specify the timing used in each comparison. The AVO index shares ATS selectivity
and its documented weight basis, while retaining a separate catchability coefficient.

The independent lognormal-index and multivariate BTS contributions had the forms

$$
\ell_s=\frac12\sum_t\frac{[\log I^{\mathrm{obs}}_{s,t}-\log\widehat I_{s,t}]^2}
{\sigma^2_{s,t}},\qquad
\ell_{\mathrm{BTS}}=\frac12\boldsymbol r^{\mathsf{T}}\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol r,
\quad r_t=\log I^{\mathrm{obs}}_t-\log\widehat I_t.
 \qquad(14)
$$

Fixed-variance normalization terms were constant for these comparisons. The normal-index option
described in 2024 instead used residuals on the original scale. The BTS covariance provided $\Sigma$
for the multivariate lognormal fit. Catch biomass enters the implemented objective as
$\lambda_C\sum_t[\log(Y_t^{\mathrm{obs}}+c)-\log(\widehat Y_t+c)]^2$, with $\lambda_C=200$ in the
retained controls. This equals $1/(2\sigma_C^2)$ for $\sigma_C=0.05$ and removed the extra factor of
two in the printed 2024 likelihood expression. Priors and penalties retain their actual source-code
weights.

### Uncertainty in mean body mass

[Ianelli et al. (2001), Section 1.14.2](#ref-ianelli2001), described calculating fishing
mortality at maximum sustainable yield within the assessment model. The [2007 assessment](#ref-ianelli2007safe)
extended that approach to propagate uncertainty in future weight-at-age. That option used
$w^{\mathrm{future}}_a\sim\mathcal{N}(\bar w_a,\sigma_{w,a}^2)$. The retained implementation fits a
mean growth curve plus cohort and year effects. For starting modeled age $a_0$, its mean curve was

$$
\bar w_a=\alpha_w\left\{L_1+(L_2-L_1)
\frac{1-K^{a-a_0}}{1-K^{A-1}}\right\}^{3}.
 \qquad(15)
$$

At the final estimation phase, the recurrence in `Est_Fixed_Effects_wts()` was

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat w_{t,a_0}&=\bar w_{a_0}
\exp(\sigma_c^2/2+\sigma_c c_t),\\
\widehat w_{t,a}&=\widehat w_{t-1,a-1}
+(\bar w_a-\bar w_{a-1})\exp(\sigma_y^2/2+\sigma_y y_t), &&a>a_0.
\end{aligned}
 \qquad(16)
$$

The initial year starts at $\bar w_a$; dataset-specific scale vectors map the latent weights to
observation series. This notation corrects the increment index in 2024 and explicitly retained the
implementation's sigma scaling and final-phase offsets. The cohort and year deviations receive
standard-normal penalties. The four-term weight objective was

$$
\ell_w=\frac12\sum_{h,t,a}
\frac{(w^{\mathrm{obs}}_{h,t,a}-\bar w_a)^2}{\sigma^2_{h,t,a}}
+\frac12\sum_{h,t,a}
\frac{(w^{\mathrm{obs}}_{h,t,a}-\widehat w_{h,t,a})^2}{\sigma^2_{h,t,a}}
+\frac12\sum_t c_t^2+\frac12\sum_t y_t^2.
 \qquad(17)
$$

The 2026 numerical baseline allocated all four terms and retained their sum.

### Tier 1 projections: historical calculation

The 2024 description retained a Tier 1 calculation based on fishable biomass, the harmonic-mean
harvest rate at MSY, and a spawning-biomass adjustment:

$$
\begin{aligned}
ABC_t&=B^f_{{\mathrm{GM}},t}\widehat u_{\mathrm{HM}}\zeta_t,\\
B^f_{{\mathrm{GM}},t}&=\exp\{\log\widehat B^f_t-\sigma^2_{\log B^f}/2\},\\
\widehat u_{\mathrm{HM}}&=\exp\{\log\widehat u_{\mathrm{MSY}}-\sigma^2_{\log u}/2\},\\
\zeta_t&=\begin{cases}
(B_t/B_{\mathrm{MSY}}-0.05)/0.95,&B_t<B_{\mathrm{MSY}},\\
1,&B_t\geq B_{\mathrm{MSY}}.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
 \qquad(18)
$$

The geometric and harmonic adjustments assume the documented lognormal approximations. This
historical formula described the earlier calculation over its applicable biomass range; final advice
used the adopted tier and the complete corresponding harvest-control rule.

### Tier 3 projections

For fixed mortality, maturity, weights and selectivity, equilibrium spawning biomass per recruit at
fishing intensity $F$ was

$$
\begin{aligned}
l_1(F)&=1,\qquad l_a(F)=l_{a-1}(F)e^{-M_{a-1}-Fs_{a-1}}, &&1<a<A,\\
l_A(F)&=\frac{l_{A-1}(F)e^{-M_{A-1}-Fs_{A-1}}}{1-e^{-M_A-Fs_A}},\\
\psi(F)&=\sum_a l_a(F)\phi_a w^s_a e^{-\tau(M_a+Fs_a)},\\
B_{100\%}&=\bar R\psi(0),\qquad
B_{x\%}=\frac{x}{100}B_{100\%},\qquad
\frac{\psi(F_{x\%})}{\psi(0)}=\frac{x}{100}.
\end{aligned}
 \qquad(19)
$$

Tier 3a used $F_{40\%}$ for maximum ABC and $F_{35\%}$ for OFL, with the adopted biomass-dependent
rule applied when needed. Projection catch followed [Equation 2](#eq-admb-catch). The 2024 SPM
calculation used one sex category split equally into females and males, fixed biological schedules
and selectivity, and stochastic recruitment generated from the historical arithmetic and harmonic
means with an inverse-Gaussian distribution. Its 1,000 simulations retained recruitment process
variability; uncertainty in fitted abundance, mean recruitment, selectivity and weights was omitted.
The saved seed was 123 in the historical SPM source.

## Appendix G FT-NIRS Age Prediction for EBS Pollock {#sec-ftnir-appendix}

Authored by: Derek Chamberlin, Esther Goldstein, Beth Matta, and Jason Conner

FT-NIRS Team: John Brogan, Jason Conner, Derek Chamberlin, Esther Goldstein, Brenna Hsieh, Beth
Matta, Jon Short

FT-NIRS predicted age from otolith spectra and associated specimen information, using traditional
microscopic ages for calibration and validation. The workflow proceeds from age prediction through
tester-age conversion to the assessment likelihood ([Table G1](#tbl-ftnir-treatment)). The 2024 and
2025 fishery age compositions used their respective independent tester-age keys applied to released
FT-NIRS predictions. The 2025 source was model a00-d3. The year-specific keys also convert biological
weight inputs ([Table G2](#tbl-ftnir-conversion-status)). Both composition series use the
assessment's identity ageing-error assumption after their selected age treatment.

Year-specific conditional keys redistribute source abundance and biomass among tester ages. Mean
weights were then calculated as converted biomass divided by converted abundance, with terminal ages
pooled using those totals. The partial 2024 fishery diagnostic leaves abundance and biomass at
FT-NIRS age 13 unallocated because the 2024 key had no pairs at that age ([Table
G3](#tbl-ftnir-fishery-2024-weights)). The selected assessment weight conversion fills the age-13
row using pooled age offsets and assigned a 100% CV to the target-age-15+ weight observation. The 2025
conversion used 668 independent tester pairs and fills the age-13 row, which had no pairs, with the
midpoint of the age-12 and age-14 conditional probabilities. The same key supplied the 2025 age
composition and weight observations ([Table G4](#tbl-ftnir-fishery-weights)).

BTS 2025 and 2026 use separate tester-age keys. The 2026 key retained 307 pairs after excluding 22
flagged pairs, with exact TMA ages 1--18 converted before ages 15--18 were pooled into 15+. Total
abundance and biomass were conserved. Converted weight SEs propagate the saved joint
abundance--weight covariance ([Table G5](#tbl-ftnir-bts-weights)). The fitted weight model retained
its existing marginal observation likelihood, and empirical-key uncertainty was excluded. Numerical
checks distinguish fitted use from the retained full-pair conversion diagnostics ([Table
G6](#tbl-ftnir-checks)).

Provisional 2026 ATS ages use the BTS age--length key (ALK) applied to expanded ATS length
distributions that extend to 0.5 m above the seafloor, followed by conversion to the TMA basis.
The full 2026 ATS age dataset was expected in 2027. Fish in length bins outside the BTS key remain
unallocated. The resulting weights also supply the 2026 AVO predictions.

### Fourier transform near-infrared spectroscopy (FT-NIRS) Overview {#sec-ftnir-overview}

Fourier transform near-infrared spectroscopy (FT-NIRS) emerged as an effective secondary age
prediction tool and had successfully been implemented in production ageing settings (Matta and
Helser, 2024), with FT-NIRS predicted ages recently being used to produce stock assessment age
composition data (Dick et al., 2025; Ianelli, 2025). FT-NIRS was a non-destructive technique that
interrogates a sample using light in the near-infrared region of the light spectrum (typically 4,000
to 12,000 cm^-1^).

Scanning with FT-NIRS produced a spectral signature of the sample based on the absorption of near
infrared light by different chemical bonds, such as C-H (aliphatic), C-H (aromatic), C-O (carboxyl),
O-H (hydroxyl), and N-H (amine and amide) (Murray and Williams, 1987). For otoliths, these spectra
capture changes in the organic protein matrix (otolin) relative to the inorganic calcium carbonate
structure. This relationship correlates strongly with fish growth and age (Passerotti et al., 2022)
and was used to develop models, calibrated with traditional microscopic ages (TMA) and FT-NIR
spectra, to predict the age of unknown samples based on their spectral signatures with an estimated
time-cost saving of 23-40% (Adamack et al., 2025). FT-NIRS was applied to estimate age for a
multitude of fish species from Australia (Wedding et al., 2014), the Mediterranean Sea (Basilone et
al., 2024), the eastern Bering Sea (Benson et al., 2023), and the Atlantic Ocean (Adamack et al.,
2025).

### Traditional Microscopic Ageing (TMA) QA/QC {#sec-ftnir-tma-qaqc}

The FT-NIRS models rely on traditional microscopic ageing (TMA) to calibrate the model, thus the
accuracy of the age predictions was directly impacted by the accuracy of the calibration ages
(Chamberlin et al., 2026). The AFSC Age and Growth Program (AGP) had a long history of ageing
walleye pollock by microscopic examination of otolith growth patterns (Matta et al., 2026) and had
employed a rigorous quality control program since 1983 (Kimura and Anderl, 2005). In TMA of pollock,
presumed annual marks ("annuli") were enumerated from the otolith surface in younger fish or from
burned or toasted otolith cross sections in older fish (Matta and Kimura, 2012; Matta et al., 2026).
The accuracy of the AGP's TMA for pollock was independently corroborated using a variety of
methods, including radiometric ageing, edge and marginal increment analysis, year-class tracking,
and captive-rearing studies (Kastelle and Kimura, 2006; Kimura et al., 2006; Kimura et al., 2007;
Lai, 1985).

To test FT-NIRS model prediction skill, random 20% subsamples of pollock otoliths from each
collection source (fishery, bottom-trawl survey, and hydroacoustic midwater trawl) were subjected to
TMA. Spectral outliers (i.e., those that predicted fish lengths outside an established threshold)
were also selected for TMA; see [FT-NIRS QA/QC below](#sec-ftnir-qaqc) for more details. Each
otolith selected for TMA was independently aged by two experienced readers. The TMA subsamples were
evaluated for inter-reader precision and bias. All discrepancies between the two readers were
resolved. Any TMA age-length outliers were reexamined, and re-aged or classified as collection
errors when appropriate (Kimura and Anderl, 2005).

### FT-NIRS QA/QC {#sec-ftnir-qaqc}

In addition to the TMA QA/QC, the FT-NIR spectra underwent a three-step QA/QC process to identify
poor quality spectra due to data collection errors, instrument issues, or otolith irregularities
such as crystallization, contamination, or fragmentation (Goldstein et al., 2024). Spectrometer
operators conducted qualitative QA/QC concurrent with data collection to identify missing data and
unusual spectra using length predictions from a species- and region-specific partial least-squares
regression (PLSR) model in comparison to observed lengths. Real-time length predictions were used to
identify transcription errors and provide assurance of proper instrument function.

Following data collection, rigorous QA/QC was conducted to identify outliers using principal
component analysis (PCA) and PLSR models developed from a multi-year collection of spectral data
from each data source (AFSC groundfish survey, AFSC hydroacoustic survey, fishery data) and
projections (PCA) and predictions (PLSR) of new data. PCA scores by scan date were used to visually
identify instrument drift. Gross spectral data outliers were identified from PCA using Hotelling's
T^2^ and Q residuals (Pomerantsev and Rodionova, 2014) and PLSR outlier analyses identified
discrepancies between spectra and specimen length by combining Hotelling's T^2^ and Q residuals
(full X-distance) and Y-distance (observed vs. predicted; Rodionova and Pomerantsev, 2020). Analyses
used a threshold of 1% to identify outliers. Outliers were then aged using traditional microscopic
methods. Once aged, outlier spectra were excluded from the final dataset if age predictions from the
MMCNN models were also outside the MMCNN 95% Monte Carlo dropout prediction intervals [discussed
below](#sec-ftnir-model).

### FT-NIRS Model {#sec-ftnir-model}

Age was predicted from FT-NIR spectra using a multimodal convolutional neural network model (MMCNN).
MMCNNs identify non-linear relationships in spectral data, incorporate additional inputs such as
fish length or capture location, and learn relevant spectral features during training. Classical
chemometric approaches such as PLS require the user to select key wavenumbers (Chen and Wang, 2019).
The MMCNN used here was an updated version of the MMCNN presented in Benson et al. (2023) and
Chamberlin et al. (2026). The MMCNN included one convolutional layer and six dense layers to predict
age from spectral and fish-length data.

The first layer of the MMCNN was the spectral input data which was fed to a 1D convolutional layer,
which acts as an automated feature extractor to identify patterns in the spectra. This output was
then processed with a Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation function to introduce nonlinearity
into the network necessary for approximating continuous functions (Brownlee, 2019; Géron, 2019). The
data were then flattened into a one-dimensional array and passed through a dense layer (all dense
layers use Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) activation). This reduced the dimensionality of the
spectral input and balances its contribution relative to the metadata. The metadata input was fed to
a dense layer, then concatenated with the spectral input layer. The output was passed through a fully
connected dense layer with ELU activation to model the interactions between spectral data and
metadata. To mitigate overfitting, 5 dropout layers follow each dense layer to randomly ignore a
subset of neurons and prevent codependency between nodes (Srivastava et al., 2014). Crucially, these
dropout layers remain active during the inference phase, a technique known as Monte Carlo (MC)
dropout, allowing the model to perform multiple forward passes per sample to generate a distribution
of age estimates and calculate Monte Carlo prediction intervals. Finally, a fully connected dense
layer with a single node and a batch normalization layer were used to produce a continuous age
estimate, allowing for loss estimation via a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) function. The model's
hyperparameters (the number of filters in the convolutional layer, the number of nodes in the
concatenated layer, learning rate, batch size and the dropout rate) were optimized using hyperband
optimization (Li et al., 2018) with early stopping.

The walleye pollock model was trained on spectra and TMA ages from 2014-2025 using an "n−1" annual
model updating approach. Under this scheme, spectral and age data from all fleets up to the year
prior to the target prediction year were included (for example, predicting 2025 fishery ages used
data from 2024 and earlier). For MMCNN training, input data were first split into development (80%)
and testing (20%) pooled using a randomly shuffled split that was stratified on fleet and year.
Samples receive a normalized weighting score based on 2 coefficients: *decay* was an integer \[1, 2,
3\] that defined the rate of exponential decay for samples based on year, and *alpha* \[0, 0.1, 0.2,
..., 1.0\] defined whether sample year or sample age frequency had more influence in weighting the
sample, with *alpha* = 1 turning decay off. This allowed for testing of whether model performance
improves when more recent calibration data or rare age classes were weighted more heavily. For
hyperparameter optimization, the development data were further split into training (90%) and
validation (10%) datasets to inform early stopping, using the previously defined sample weights. For
each scenario a series of 10 trainings, with random seeds, were run to estimate the median number of
epochs needed to train the model but avoid overfitting, prior to a final training run based on the
median number of epochs.

In total, 31 training models were produced with a grid search for the 2 sample weighting
coefficients, and age predictions were generated for bottom trawl survey, hydroacoustic survey and
fishery fleets. The final candidate model for each fleet was selected using four statistical
metrics: Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (Lin's CCC), the mean Winkler score, R^2^, and
the slope of the regression between FT-NIRS predicted ages and corresponding TMA ages. Lin's CCC
measures how closely the observed data aligned with a 45° line of perfect agreement, while the mean
Winkler score evaluated average performance based on the width of the Monte Carlo prediction
intervals and the frequency of samples falling outside them. The four metrics capture different
aspects of model accuracy, and visual assessments complemented them. Ultimately, the best-performing
model was identified by synthesizing these visual and quantitative criteria. Age predictions were
then finalized by removing any samples that were both flagged as a spectral outlier and an outlier
from the Monte Carlo prediction intervals. This finalized dataset was then transmitted to end users
and coded as FT-NIRS predicted ages.

### Age conversion and assessment use {#sec-ftnir-treatment}

The assessment used year-specific independent tester TMA conversions for the 2024 and 2025 fishery
compositions, matching annual weight conversions and separate survey-specific age conversions
([Table G1](#tbl-ftnir-treatment)). These treatments serve different purposes: predicting age from
spectra, allocating abundance and biomass among ages, and specifying the assessment likelihood were
separate steps. Current input and fit records establish their use; the retained partial-conversion
diagnostics document which source ages had calibration pairs and how the diagnostic quantified uncertainty.

The 2026 BTS conditional tester-age key excluded calibration pairs marked `nir_outlier = Y`,
removing 22 of 329 complete pairs and retaining 307. It targets independent `test_age` conditional
on FT-NIRS `final_nir_age`; each FT-NIRS row was normalized by its retained paired count. Conversion
used exact TMA ages 1--18 before pooling ages 15--18 into 15+. Screening applied to calibration
pairs, preserving the released abundance vector. All unflagged complete pairs were eligible,
including checks outside the systematic 20% sample.

Screening changed the exact mean converted age from 5.318978 to 5.316448 years, with a largest
age-proportion change of approximately 0.124 percentage points and unchanged total abundance. The
same 307-pair key supplied BTS weight means and their joint-covariance delta-method SEs, provisional
ATS age allocations and biomass-derived weights, and the 2026 AVO prediction weights. The standalone
RE-WAA refit and assessment fits using these inputs were complete [S10](#ftnir-source-s10). The 2025
BTS key was unchanged. The original 329-pair products remain historical evidence. Empirical-key
uncertainty was excluded; the fitted weight model retained its existing marginal observation
likelihood rather than using the full converted covariance as a new likelihood.

The contribution described 31 MMCNN training candidates, distinguished by sample-weight settings
and fleet-specific selection. PCA and PLSR provide spectral QA/QC; PLSR also provided length
predictions. The `a00-d3` and `a03-d1` labels on the [saved 600-fish
comparison](https://bookish-chainsaw-o8jopw4.pages.github.io/ftnir-prediction-overlay.html) identify
prediction sets, separately from the assessment's cumulative `0.x` input sequence.

#### Predictive model and assessment input differences {#sec-ftnir-model-levels}

The MMCNN combined spectral and fish-length information, MC dropout prediction intervals, hyperband
optimization and 31 sample-weight settings. Its annual n−1 updating rule used information available
before the prediction year; for example, a 2025 prediction used data through 2024. The selected
fleet-by-year model checksum, coefficient setting and exact mapping to the saved 600-fish prediction
files remain to be documented.

The full tester-key release used `final_nir_age` as predictor and independent `test_age` as target,
excluding resolved `final_age` as the calibration target. It contained 3,000 fishery-2025 records,
1,638 BTS-2025 records and 1,586 BTS-2026 records; 2,992, 1,619 and 1,582 released FT-NIRS
ages. Their complete-pair counts were 668, 390 and 329, respectively; the screened 2026 BTS
application retained 307 [S1](#ftnir-source-s1).

For the 2025 fishery, model a00-d3 FT-NIRS ages were converted to independent tester ages using the
668 complete paired observations. The conditional probability of tester age $j$ given FT-NIRS age
$i$ was $K_{ij}=n_{ij}/\sum_j n_{ij}$. Converted numbers were $N^{\mathrm{TMA}}_j=\sum_i
N^{\mathrm{FTNIR}}_iK_{ij}$. Empirical rows retain the released paired observations, including
flagged pairs. FT-NIRS age 13 had no paired tester ages. Its conversion probabilities use the
midpoint of the age-12 and age-14 rows, $K_{13,j}=(K_{12,j}+K_{14,j})/2$, giving probabilities of one third at tester age 10, one sixth at age 11 and one half at age 15. The age-12
row had six pairs and the age-14 row had one pair.
Source and tester ages in the release were exact ages 2--15; the assessment terminal group contained
ages 15 and older. The selected likelihood sample size was 530. The key was treated as fixed;
empirical-key and interpolation uncertainty were excluded.

The 2024 fishery composition used its 693-pair independent tester key. FT-NIRS age 13 had no
paired tester ages. Its conversion row used pooled TMA-minus-FT-NIRS offsets from the same
year's source ages 9--12 (34 pairs).
Empirical rows remain unchanged; the selected likelihood input was 578. Both recent years were
converted before fitting and use a 15-by-15 identity ageing-error matrix, equivalent to the ADMB
setting with ageing error switched off. Key and tail-allocation uncertainty were additional to the
sampling precision represented by the selected likelihood weights.

Weight conversion applied the same conditional key to source numbers and biomass, then divides
converted biomass by converted numbers. Terminal-age weights use pooled totals. The partial
empirical 2024 diagnostic leaves abundance and biomass at FT-NIRS age 13 unallocated. The selected weight
treatment fills that row using pooled offsets from source ages 9--12 and assigned a 100% CV to the
target-age-15+ observation. Those fixed approximations add no empirical calibration pairs; their
uncertainty differed from a sampling SE. The 2025 weight observations use the same source-age-13
midpoint as the age composition. Their zero-abundance source-age-1 padding contributed no converted
numbers or biomass. The midpoint was specific to 2025; source age 14 also lacks pairs in the 2024
key.

The older staging record [S6](#ftnir-source-s6) described a 2024 endpoint in `pm_26_candidate.dat`:
fishery CAA at 0.4, provisional BTS WAA/biomass at 0.5/0.6, ATS at 0.7, and separate AVO-only
0.8/0.9 components. These were historical input-sequence labels from the [incremental-model
plan](https://bookish-chainsaw-o8jopw4.pages.github.io/incremental-models-2026.html). Current fitted
use followed the documented working input and run records, not those earlier staging exclusions.

#### Source and validation limits {#sec-ftnir-treatment-pending}

The partial 2024 empirical diagnostic keeps abundance and biomass at FT-NIRS age 13 unallocated. Selected
assessment weights use the pooled-offset rule and 100% CV described above. The 2024 and 2025
compositions use their respective tester-age keys and the age-13 allocation rules described above. Weight SEs propagate
the available joint abundance--weight covariance, while the fitted model retained its marginal
observation likelihood. Empirical-key uncertainty remained excluded.

The assessment author identified a00-d3 as the selected 2025 fishery model. The exact training-run
checksum, coefficient setting and complete collection-by-year release record remain to be
documented. The 31 predictive candidates and the assessment's cumulative input stages identify
different choices. The earlier mixed-basis BTS workbook remained unavailable; the separately
identified current workbook was excluded from assessment assembly. Its source basis must be
established before using it in a comparison.

Provisional ATS products retain their transferred BTS age--length and tester-age keys,
length-bin coverage of the BTS key and separate sampling conditions. Direct ATS age and weight validation
remained open, with the full 2026 ATS age dataset expected in 2027. Archived full-pair calibration products
remain available alongside the screened-key input records. Prior fit, projection and posterior
records retain their original dates and input identities. Final model and recommendation selection
remain separate review decisions.

### Year-specific weight-conversion diagnostics {#sec-ftnir-weight-patterns}

The retained full-pair conversion record separated three completed year-specific conversions from
the partial 2024 fishery diagnostic ([conversion-status table](#adj-tbl-conversion-status)). Fishery
2025 and BTS 2025--2026 use independent tester-age keys. The partial 2024 fishery diagnostic
leaves abundance and biomass at FT-NIRS age 13 unallocated.

Mean weights generally increase with age, with the largest source-versus- converted differences
concentrated at older ages ([2024 fishery weight table](#adj-tbl-fishery-2024-weights)). The partial
fishery 2024 values at TMA ages 13 and 14 were both 1.2878 kg, while its target 15+ weight remained
missing. Its prepared older-age SEs were large relative to the means; the partial converted SDs
condition on the fixed key and source ages with paired observations.

The 2025 fishery conversion raises the 15+ mean from 0.8102 to 1.2676 kg; target ages 13 and 14
retain missing weights because converted abundance was zero ([fishery weight
comparison](#adj-tbl-fishery-weights)). Conversion changes both which older ages had weight estimates and the values of those estimates.

BTS 2025 converted weights were generally below the source weights from age 5 upward; in 2026,
weights at ages 3--8 remain close to or above their source values, while older-age weights were lower
([BTS weight comparison](#adj-tbl-bts-weights); [Figure G1](#fig-ftnir-assessment-weights)). The 15+
mean changes from 1.7646 to 1.5474 kg in 2025 and from 1.8390 to 1.3665 kg in 2026. These were
conversion contrasts that vary by age and year. The smaller conditional SEs in several converted
cells retain the stated fixed-key uncertainty scope.

Independent fishery arithmetic, preservation of earlier fishery values and survey
covariance/derivative checks establish computational consistency ([conversion
checks](#adj-tbl-checks)). The partial 2024 diagnostic leaves abundance and biomass at FT-NIRS age 13 unallocated. Current selected weights use the separate pooled-offset tail treatment and 100% CV, and
the screened-key standalone RE-WAA and assessment fits were complete. These distinctions preserve the
historical diagnostic's restriction to ages with paired observations and the current fit's fixed-key uncertainty scope.

#### Conversion and approved approximations {#adj-conversion-and-approved-approximations}

Each key gave the distribution of TMA tester age conditional on FTNIR age. Abundance and biomass
were redistributed together, using the same conditional probabilities. Converted mean weight was
converted biomass divided by converted abundance. Within a source FTNIR bin, this calculation
assigned the same source mean weight to every target age.

For fishery 2025, Jim approved two rules for source ages without paired tester observations:

- Age 1: a dummy identity row assigned FTNIR age 1 to TMA age 1. All saved source age-1 catch estimates were zero, so this row retained zero catch.
- Age 13: each target-age probability was the arithmetic average of its probabilities in the source age-12 and age-14 rows. The resulting row sums to one. This approximation used the existing age-12 and age-14 pairs.

Converted target-age 13 and 14 abundances were zero in the 2025 fishery key. Their weights and SEs
remain paired missing observations. The historical data continue to inform these ages in the future
wtAgeRE fit. All pre-2025 fishery mean/SE decimal values were preserved exactly.

Exact BTS target ages 1--18 were retained during conversion. Target ages 15--18 were then pooled into
15+, conserving total abundance and biomass. The 2024 fishery key also retained exact target ages
through 18; the 2025 fishery key had target ages through 15. The same terminal pooling convention
applied. Age selection for wtAgeRE occurs after conversion; its input bins were 3--15+.

#### Fishery 2024 results and remaining gap {#adj-fishery-2024-results-and-remaining-gap}

The recovered 2024 release contained 2,985 released FTNIR ages and 693 complete independent tester
pairs. The target was `test_age`; the resolved `final_age` was a separate field. Canonical specimen
and age-field hashes match the independent original-workbook verification record. The original
workbook itself remained outside this local snapshot. The empirical key used all complete released
pairs, including additional QA/QC selections; their representativeness remained an assumption.

Source ages 1--12 had empirical probability rows. Source ages 13--15 lack pairs; only age

abundance and 0.0817% of biomass. Allocated plus unallocated totals balance across all 1,001
saved rows to relative errors below 6.7e-16. The diagnostic retained that mass separately and

The table and figure report the partial, fixed-key bootstrap mean and SD from source ages with paired tester observations. Every converted 2024 bin remained conditional on the unresolved source-age-13
allocation. Target TMA age 15+ receives zero allocated abundance, so its mean and SD remain missing.
Source FTNIR age 13 and target TMA age 13 were distinct: other source ages with paired tester observations can contribute to target ages 13 and 14.

The 2025 midpoint rule stays specific to its approved key. In 2024, source age 14 also lacks
calibration pairs; applying the age-12/14 midpoint rule would require calibration pairs at age 14.
The 2024 key included pairs at source age 1 and retained its catch.

will be applied in 2027.

## Appendix H BTS Spatiotemporal Biomass Index and Abundance at Age, Including the Northern Bering Sea {#sec-bts-spatiotemporal-appendix}

This appendix described the spatiotemporal modeling approach used to estimate the bottom-trawl
survey (BTS) biomass index and abundance at age for the combined eastern and northern Bering Sea
(EBS and NBS). This approach was adopted in the 2024 assessment for both abundance at age and survey
indices and followed the approach used by the AFSC Groundfish Assessment Program (GAP) in previous
assessments. The sections below describe its application to the 2026 survey data, including model
specifications and uncertainty estimates.

### Scope and relationship to the earlier VAST appendix

The earlier VAST appendix described a different software generation and mixed 1982--2023/2024
coverage. It was retained as a historical source. The description used the settings in the saved
production fit objects. The saved production fit objects identify sdmTMB 1.0.0 for the biomass
index and tinyVAST 1.6.3 for abundance at age. Model-based integration across EBS and NBS
extended the approach used to address pollock distribution shifts ([O'Leary et al.
2020](#ref-OLeary2020)). The sdmTMB framework was described by Anderson et al.
([2022](#ref-Anderson2022)).

Both output series contain 44 years, 1982--2019 and 2021--2026. The survey was absent in 2020.
The index fit retained 2020 as an additional latent time step representing a model prediction. The
age fit retained annual time levels across 1982--2026, while the abundance and composition data files
omit 2020. NBS sampling coverage varied among years within the prediction domain.

### Biomass index

The pollock index code reads density-dependence-corrected station biomass density from the
VAST-named input file. The file name was historical; the saved model class was sdmTMB. Input density
was converted from kg/ha to kg/km² by multiplying by 100. The saved fit used a Poisson-link
delta-gamma observation model with separate year effects and spatial and spatiotemporal fields. Both
components had spatial fields and annual AR(1) spatiotemporal structure. The retained call enables
geometric anisotropy and included a spatially varying coefficient for the environmental covariate.

The companion pollock code defined that covariate as standardized cold-pool area, the area of bottom
water at or below 2°C ([Rohan et al. 2022](#ref-rohan2022)). The saved object contained its numerical
covariate and the formula; the complete annual cold-pool release manifest remained unavailable. The
exact environmental release and production script revision require confirmation.

Predicted density was integrated over a fixed regional grid. For grid-cell area (A\_{r,j}) in km² and
predicted biomass density (d\_{t,j}) in kg/km², the regional biomass index in tons was

$$
\widehat I_{r,t}=\frac{1}{1000}\sum_{j\in r}A_{r,j}\widehat d_{t,j}.
 \qquad(20)
$$

The biomass-index estimates include separate EBS, NBS and combined Both products. The combined
2026 point estimate was 9,034,017.809 t; the separate EBS and NBS point estimates sum to that
value within numerical precision. These survey estimates remain subject to assessment input
selection and acceptance.

### Abundance at age

The saved tinyVAST fit used numerical density at station and age, with age-by-year fixed effects in
both delta components. All 15 labelled age classes had age-specific spatial variance terms and a
common estimated lag-1 temporal coefficient in the spatiotemporal specification. The saved control
had anisotropy disabled. This model used age-by-year effects with the environmental terms excluded.

The companion pollock code multiplies CPUE_num by 100, converting fish/ha to fish/km². Its comment
describing this as a conversion of kg was inconsistent with the numerical input; the calculation was
an abundance calculation. Numerical density was integrated over the combined EBS--NBS grid and scaled
to billions of fish:

$$
\widehat N_{r,t,a}\;[\mathrm{billion\ fish}]
=\frac{1}{10^9}\sum_{j\in r}A_{r,j}\widehat n_{t,a,j},
\qquad
\widehat p_{r,t,a}=
\frac{\widehat N_{r,t,a}}{\sum_b\widehat N_{r,t,b}}.
 \qquad(21)
$$

The abundance-at-age matrix contained 15 rows and 44 year columns. Its row order agrees with the
companion age_1 through age_15 composition columns: normalizing every matrix column reproduced the
composition file to a maximum absolute difference of (8.4\^{-16}). The 2026 combined total was
16.064690 billion fish. The companion composition file supplied the age labels for the matrix
and must remain attached to it. Displayed ages were 1--14 and 15+; the terminal category represented
fish aged 15 and older. The original source column names were retained in the data. The age export
supplied only the combined EBS--NBS estimates (terminal-age interpretation).

These expanded compositions use the age assignments and age--length-key preparation in their
station-level inputs. Age assignment and FT-NIRS-to-traditional-age conversion precede the tinyVAST
expansion. The exact release, assignment rules for 2025--2026, and any age-age correction used in
this production input remain part of the source reconciliation.

### Verified settings and prediction-code evidence

The retained index fit used 250 interior mesh knots, anisotropy and a spatially varying
environmental coefficient; the age fit used 50 interior knots with anisotropy disabled and a
separate spatial variance structure by age ([Table H1](#tbl-bts-spatial-settings)). Prediction-grid
and integration settings were identified separately as companion-code evidence. The local code
checkout was 2a9e6f26062d34ee0375f8eac9462e51273e65a3. Its default species selections were Pacific cod
for the index and yellowfin sole for age compositions. The saved pollock fit objects supply the
production evidence for this appendix; the generic default selections remain code context.

::: {#tbl-bts-spatial-settings .report-table .unnumbered data-table="tables/086-tbl-bts-spatial-settings.csv"}

Table H1 Delivered 2026 Pollock Fit and Companion Prediction Settings

:::

::: {.table-notes}
*Note.* Retained settings in the 2026 pollock fit objects, with prediction-grid and integration settings identified separately as companion-code evidence. The complete production prediction record remains unavailable.
:::

The code grid had 492,989.921 km² in the EBS and 198,866.805 km² in the NBS, summing to 691,856.726
km². Those grid files were hashed in the source record. The complete production prediction grid and
expansion invocation remain unavailable. This draft therefore distinguished companion-code settings
from verified saved-fit settings. The historical 2-nmi grid and 750-knot index describe the earlier
VAST workflow.

### Uncertainty, diagnostics and outstanding review

The index code requests bias-corrected integration. It also contained a 500-simulation covariance
workflow. The assessment selects its covariance file and uncertainty treatment separately from those
integration settings. The age expansion code sets bias.correct=FALSE and getsd=FALSE despite
apply.epsilon=TRUE. Its age output therefore excluded epsilon bias correction and a full estimated
age-composition covariance. Assessment weighting and the selected design-based covariance remain
separate decisions.

The saved index object reports a positive definite Hessian and maximum absolute retained gradient
0.0138148. The saved age object reports optimizer return code 0, a positive definite Hessian and
maximum retained gradient 0.000205084. These diagnostics required provider review for numerical
acceptance. Both gradients exceed the workspace's (10\^{-4}) assessment-model convergence guardrail;
their suitability for these survey fits required provider review. This appendix used the saved
survey fits by the provider.

The saved index data had 17,236 rows, while the adjacent raw index export had 17,237; the
counts differ in 2026 (350 versus 351). The saved age fit had 265,350 rows, versus 258,555
in the adjacent age-density export. Historical differences occur in 1982, 1985, 1988, 1991, 1994,
2001, 2005, 2006 and 2018; 2026 had 5,250 fitted rows versus 5,265 exported rows. These differences
prevent a claim that the saved objects exactly reproduce the neighboring raw files. Their causes,
the intended final input versions and the fit-to-export chain require confirmation from the survey
analysts.

Before finalizing this appendix, confirm the production script revision, prediction grid, annual
environmental release, full R/TMB/dependency versions, age-assignment lineage, treatment of the
input mismatches, and the accepted covariance and diagnostic assessment. The latest linked general
writeup and terms-of-reference table remain unavailable through the connected source. Their
agreement with this draft required author review. Historical VAST dependency versions retain their
original dates.

### Source and reproducibility record

The local provenance bundle retained saved-object metadata and checks, source file hashes, output
consistency checks, and the read-only extraction scripts. It also preserved the original historical
VAST text and historical PDF. The original fit objects and station-level inputs remain in their
owning data directory. The report consumes saved metadata and aggregate outputs.

and [age-composition
workflow](https://github.com/afsc-gap-products/model-based-indices/blob/2a9e6f26062d34ee0375f8eac9462e51273e65a3/R/bs_age_comps.R).
Author-documents awaiting access: [general methods
writeup](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nZhbF4GNNDy0JBcmXs8RcGfREV0AiDN-i06PUSkFcKI/edit) and
[terms-of-reference

## Appendix I Assessment Development and Supporting Record {#review-and-source-record}

The September 2026 assessment development document ([Ianelli et al.
2026](#ref-ianelli2026developments)), published 3 September, presents the starting model comparisons
and exploratory appendices using data through 2024. Corrected through-2024 results were archived with
that document; the main assessment used observations through 2026.

The Plan Team excerpt provided the seven recommendation summaries ([Table A1](#tbl-plan-team)). Its
final report citation and any subsequent SSC direction require verification before release.

The source guidelines were *Alaska Groundfish Stock Assessment Guidelines*, July 2024, in a file
named *Stock Assessment Guidelines Tier 3.docx*. Their publication procedures inform eventual
release preparation. The development copy remained local under the user's release timing.
